Lesson 16: Staying At a Hotel 
Nolan and Beth are a married couple who are staying at a hotel on vacation. Listen to 
their conversation and answer these question: 
Listening Comprehension 
1. The hotel that Nolan and Beth are staying at is... 
a. a luxury hotel 
b. a run-down hotel 
c. a simple hotel 
 
2. Nolan's main complaint is about... 
a. the price 
b. the room 
c. the service 
 
3. What is included with their stay? 
a. drinks at the bar 
b. meals in the restaurant 
c. a free tour of the city 
 
4. Beth comments on the beauty of the... 
a. artwork 
b. chandelier 
c. furniture 
 
5. Nolan is upset because... 
a. he didn't get a discount 
b. his bags were lost at the airport 
c. the hotel doesn't have a swimming pool 
 
 
 


 
 
6. They are currently vacationing in... 
a. Chicago 
b. London 
c. Paris 
 
7. At the end of the conversation, Beth decides to go to... 
a. the bar 
b. the beauty parlor 
c. the restaurant 
 
8. Nolan says they shouldn't go out because... 
a. he and Beth are angry at each other 
b. it's late at night 
c. the hotel is far from everything 
 
9. Tomorrow they are going to... 
a. change hotels 
b. go shopping 
c. see the sights 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Nolan: We’re really paying through the nose 
for this hotel! 
Beth: Nolan, please don’t start griping about 
the price. We’re on vacation – now’s not the 
time to pinch pennies. 
Nolan: Yeah, but we’re shelling out two 
thousand bucks for a week here. We’ll be 
broke by the end of our trip. 
Beth: After a whole year of working like dogs, 
don’t we deserve to treat ourselves to 
something nice? Besides, there’s a gourmet 
restaurant, and the meals are included with the 
price of our room.  
Nolan: Hmph… “gourmet” usually means you 
pay top dollar for a tiny portion – arranged all 
artistically on the plate, of course. 
Beth: Oh, you just don’t know how to appreciate 
the finer things in life. 
Nolan: I can appreciate them… as long as I can 
have seconds… 
paying through the nose = 
paying a LOT of money 
(often too much for what 
you are getting) 
griping = complaining 
pinch pennies = try to save 
every little bit of money 
shelling out = spending (a 
large amount of money) 
bucks = dollars 
be broke = have no money 
available 
working like dogs = working 
very hard, at a job that’s 
difficult or unpleasant 
treat ourselves = give 
ourselves something nice 
gourmet = fancy, very nice 
quality 
top dollar = a high price 
portion = amount of food 
seconds = a second portion 
of food after you have 
finished the first portion 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Beth: I’m sure the meals are delicious and 
filling, Nolan. Will you stop being so grumpy? 
Just look at this lobby. It’s so elegant with all 
the antique furniture. 
Nolan: Probably fake. 
Beth: Be that as it may, it’s still gorgeous. And 
you did brag about our room to your pals back 
in Chicago. 
Nolan: Well, yeah. But the daily rate is still 
highway robbery. 
Beth: You’re just sulking because you didn’t get 
the discount you wanted. I told you it wasn’t 
valid here in Paris.  
Nolan: But it was at our hotel in London last 
year! I can’t believe this place refused to take 
my Community Club discount. We do a lot of 
work for charity. Is it too much to ask that we 
get 10% off travel expenses? 
Beth: Well, then our next trip will be in the U.S. 
– how about to a log cabin in the middle of 
nowhere? Then at least you’d get your precious 
discount. 
filling = substantial; have 
enough substance to satisfy 
your hunger 
grumpy = in a bad mood 
lobby = the 
reception/waiting area of 
the hotel 
antique = very old 
be that as it may = even if 
what you say is true 
gorgeous = very beautiful 
brag about = speak 
arrogantly about 
pals = friends 
highway robbery = the 
charging of a ridiculous high 
fee or price 
sulking = be angry and 
withdrawn because of 
something bad or unfair 
that happened 
is it too much to ask = this 
is not unreasonable 
in the middle of nowhere = 
in a very isolated place 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Nolan: Hey, no need to get snippy! All I said 
was that two thousand dollars is a lot… but now 
that we’ve already paid, I guess we should 
make the most of it. 
Beth: Exactly. I’m going to go get a manicure at 
the beauty parlor. Why don’t you wait for me in 
the bar? Have yourself a drink, maybe it’ll help 
you loosen up. Afterwards we’ll try the 
restaurant.  
Nolan: Geez, are you planning on seeing Paris at 
all, or just spending the whole time in the hotel? 
Beth: You’re impossible! Why do you always – 
Nolan: Hey, don’t jump down my throat! I was 
just messing with you. It’s too late to go out 
now, anyway. We’ll just unwind tonight and 
then get an early start on our sightseeing 
tomorrow morning.

can be “sharp” and hurtful 
make the most of it = get 
the most advantage out of 
this situation 
manicure = having one’s 
fingernails cared for and 
painted 
loosen up = relax, be more 
friendly and less tense 
jump down my throat = 
suddenly and strongly 
criticize, disagree with, or 
get angry at someone 
messing with you = 
bothering/annoying you 
unwind = become relaxed 
after being stressed or 
tense

3. I know this project isn't much fun, but _________________________, we should still 
try to do a good job. 
4. Last year I took a pay cut, and now I'm _________________________ in order to pay

playing pranks. 
6. My father bought my mother a _________________________ necklace for their 
anniversary - it's gold with tiny emeralds in it.

_________________________ about even the smallest inconveniences. 
8. She won first place in the singing competition, and hasn't stopped 
_________________________  it ever since. 
9. The company my uncle started ended up failing, and he found himself 
_________________________ and jobless with a family to support. 
10. Pete has been _________________________ all summer - sometimes from 7 AM to 7 
PM without a break. 


 
 
11. We only have an hour to chat, so let's _________________________ and get straight 
to the point. 
12. When I was a kid and my parents took away my video games, I would spend 
hours in my room _________________________. 
13. The _________________________ at this cafe are pretty big, so we can order a single 
dish and split it.

What would you do? Who would you travel with? Let your imagination run wild!

Lesson 17: A Mysterious Movie 
Listen to Paula and Jack discuss the movie they just saw, and answer the comprehension 
questions based on their conversation: 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Paula thought the movie was... 
a. boring 
b. disturbing 
c. great 
2. The killer was... 
a. a history teacher 
b. a high school student 
c. a man wearing black 
3. How many people were killed? 
a. six 
b. sixteen 
c. sixty 
4. The real events took place in... 
a. 1964 
b. 1974 
c. 1984 
5. One thing the movie didn't explain was... 
a. how the killer escaped 
b. what motivated the murders 
c. where the bodies were hidden 
6. Jack was frightened by the movie because... 
a. he knew one of the people who was killed 
b. he misjudged one of the characters 
c. it showed a lot of blood and gruesome images 
7. Paula is determined to... 
a. find out more about the case 
b. launch a career as a detective 
c. see the movie's sequel 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Jack: That movie was weird, don’t you think? 
Paula: What do you mean? I thought it was 
terrific. It’s not often you see a movie with 
such a great twist at the end.  
Jack: But that’s what makes it so creepy. I 
was positive the man in the black suit was the 
killer, but it turned out to be the high school 
history teacher, Mrs. Kepler.  
Paula: I was really thrown for a loop. Mrs. 
Kepler seemed so sweet, there was nothing 
sinister about her whatsoever. But she was 
killing off the faculty, one by one. You know, 
on the way out of the theater I overheard 
someone saying the movie was based on a 
true story. 
Jack: No way! If there was a killing spree like 
that, we would have heard about it. I mean 
come on, she killed sixteen people, that kinda 
thing would have been all over the news. 
Paula: I didn’t say the case was recent. The 
person was saying it all went down in a small 
European town in 1974. The writer dug up 
the story when he visited Europe. He just 
changed a few details to make the movie more 
dramatic. 
Jack: Ugh! I’ll never look at a history teacher 
the same way again.  
Paula: The real mystery was her motive. The 
movie left us hanging on that part. Now I’m 
weird = strange, unusual 
twist = unexpected change of 
events 
creepy = produces a sensation 
of uneasiness or fear 
I was thrown for a loop = 
completely surprised and upset 
sinister = threatening or 
suggesting evil 
faculty = group of teachers at a 
school or college 
overheard = heard part of 
someone else’s conversation 
a killing spree = a lot of people 
killed in a short amount of time 
it all went down = a slang way 
to say “it all happened” 
dug up the story = searched 
for & discovered some hidden 
or little-known information 
left us hanging = didn’t fully 
explain it; left us in suspense 
Vocabulary 


 
 
going to look up the case. What was Mrs. 
Kepler’s background? What drove her to kill so 
many people?  
Jack: Maybe there was no reason. Could be she 
was just an evil person masquerading as a 
kind, motherly teacher. I don’t understand why 
you’re so intrigued by these cases. 
Paula: But aren’t you curious?  
Jack: Paula, when Mrs. Kepler confessed, it 
made my blood turn cold. I really pegged her 
as a harmless old lady who wouldn’t hurt a fly. 
I was fooled, and that scares me. I would have 
trusted Mrs. Kepler, just like those people in the 
movie did – and I would have ended up six feet 
under, too. And that’s what makes me shudder. 
Paula: We also gotta find out who the man in 
black was. The movie never revealed his 
identity. 
Jack: Uh-oh. I can see by that look on your face 
that you’re not going to leave me alone unless I 
help you research this movie. 
Paula: There are still so many loose ends in the 
story! Mrs. Kepler was pretty old and frail – 
how did she manage to hide the bodies? Hey – 
the man in black might have been Mrs. Kepler’s 
accomplice. He could still be prowling the 
streets… just lurking in the dark until he finds 
his next victim… 
Jack: Don’t say that – now I’m gonna have 
nightmares for sure!  
 
drove her = motivated her 
masquerading as = 
pretending to be 
intrigued = extremely 
interested 
made my blood turn cold = 
caused an intense sensation 
of fear 
pegged her = an informal 
way to say “classified her” 
wouldn’t hurt a fly = would 
not hurt anyone 
fooled = deceived 
six feet under = (slang) dead 
shudder = shake with fear 
loose ends = unresolved 
issues 
frail = weak 
accomplice = partner/helper 
in a crime 
prowling = going around 
looking for a victim 
lurking = existing unobserved 
nightmares = scary dreams 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz

____________________________.

hadn't eaten for weeks. 
3. It was supposed to be a surprise party, but I knew about it because I 
____________________________ my sister talking about it on the phone. 
4. Losing his parents to cancer at a young age was what ____________________________

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 18: Childhood 
Nora and Jolene are chatting about their experiences as children. Listen to their 
conversation and choose the best answer for each question: 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Nora describes the accidents she had at... 
a. a birthday party 
b. her school 
c. the circus 
2. Jolene's case of mistaken identity happened at... 
a. a gas station 
b. a grocery store 
c. a restaurant 
3. When Jolene stayed up late, she used to... 
a. eat snacks 
b. play outside 
c. read in bed 
4. Nora got in trouble when she... 
a. appeared to be missing 
b. broke something inside a closet 
c. made too much noise and woke her parents up 
5. Jolene usually wasn't punished because... 
a. her behavior was good 
b. her father was lenient 
c. her parents didn't find out about what she did 
6. After school, Nora would... 
a. accompany her mother to various places 
b. attend sports practice 
c. do homework for several hours 
7. How did Nora feel about summer camp? 
a. she loved it 
b. she hated it 
c. she sometimes liked it, and sometimes didn't like it 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Nora: I was so clumsy when I was a kid. 
There was this one time my family went to the 
circus, and I remember tumbling down three 
flights of stairs, crashing into the popcorn 
seller, and finally colliding with a girl eating 
ice cream.  
Jolene: Yikes! Yeah, I was pretty 
uncoordinated, too. Did you ever mistake 
strangers for your parents? 
 
Nora: No. Did you? 
 
Jolene: A bunch of times. Once I was in the 
grocery store, and my mom was busy 
rearranging the food in our cart. I saw this 
dark-haired man leaning into a freezer to 
grab some frozen meals. He looked just like 
my dad from the back. So I ran up to him, 
hugged him and said “hi dad!” When he 
turned around, both of us were startled.  
 
Nora: I can imagine! Did you ever stay up 
past your bedtime when you were a kid? 
 
Jolene: You bet. I would turn off my lights, 
then go under my bed sheets with a flashlight 
to read or do coloring books.  
 
Nora: Sometimes me and my two brothers 
would sneak out of our rooms and play hide 
and seek in the dark. We’d have to wait till 
about midnight, to be sure my parents were 
sound asleep.  
clumsy = not graceful or 
physically coordinated; always 
having accidents 
tumbling down = falling in a 
disorganized way 
flights of stairs = each section 
of stairs going from one floor 
to another is called a “flight” 
Yikes! = an expression of 
surprise or mild shock 
A bunch of = several; many 
leaning = inclining the body 
startled = mildly frightened or 
shocked 
stay up = remain awake 
You bet = definitely 
sneak out = go out in a quiet, 
secret way 
hide and seek = a game 
where some people hide and 
one person looks for them 
sound asleep = sleeping 
deeply; not likely to wake up 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Jolene: Sounds like fun! But did you ever 
get in trouble? 
 
Nora: Yeah, one time when I dozed off 
while hiding in a closet. My brothers 
couldn’t find me, so they gave up and went 
to bed. Then in the morning, my mom saw I 
wasn’t in my room and she flipped out. 
 
 
Jolene: That’s funny! Well, not so much for 
your mom at the time. But I’m sure she was 
glad you were all right. 
 
Nora: Of course she was – but we still got 
punished. All three of us were grounded 
for a week – and we had to do extra chores.  
 
Jolene: I usually managed to weasel out of 
getting punished. My mom was pretty strict, 
but my dad was a total pushover. Every 
time I pleaded with him to let me off the 
hook, he’d eventually give in. It used to 
drive my mom up the wall. 
 
Nora: That definitely wouldn’t fly with my 
parents. When it came to decisions 
involving us kids, they backed each other 
up. 
 
dozed off = fell asleep 
gave up = stopped, desisted 
flipped out = became very upset 
and agitated 
glad = happy 
grounded = a punishment where 
kids/teenagers are not allowed 
to leave the house to meet their 
friends or do fun things 
chores = obligatory tasks 
(especially housework) 
weasel out of = escape an 
obligation in a deceptive way 
a pushover = someone who is 
easily persuaded 
pleaded with = asked with a lot 
of emotion 
give in = stop resisting and agree 
to do what someone else wants 
you to 
drive my mom up the wall = 
make her very annoyed 
wouldn’t fly = wouldn’t work 
backed each other up = 
supported each other 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Jolene: Sometimes I wish I could turn back 
the clock and be a kid again. I used to roam 
around the neighborhood without a care 
in the world.  
Nora: Not me. After picking me up from 
school, my mom would drag me along on 
all her errands.  
Jolene: Bummer. What about during the 
summers, did you ever go to summer camp? 
Nora: Every year! I think my parents sent

But it was awesome, we got to do stuff like

Lesson 19: The Times are Changing 
Noel is looking for a job, but he’s not having much success. His friend Tori tries to give 
him support and advice. Listen to their conversation and mark these statements as 
“True” or “False.” 
Listening Comprehension 
Are these statements true or false according to the dialogue? 
1. Noel dressed nicely for the interview. 
2. Tori was surprised to hear he wasn't hired. 
3. Noel thought it would be difficult to get the job. 
4. Noel was an excellent student. 
5. Mitch read Noel's resume carefully. 
6. Noel talked too much during the interview. 
7. Mitch rejected Noel because he didn't have enough experience. 
8. Tori is sympathetic to Noel's feelings. 
9. Tori's job also requires staying up-to-date. 
10. Tori offers to help Noel get a job at her company. 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Tori: Hey Noel, you’re looking sharp today! 
But why the long face?  
Noel: I just got back from a job interview, and it 
was nothing but a waste of time.  
Tori: Sorry to hear that. Was this the RN job at 
Medical Alliance?  
Noel: Yup. 
Tori: What happened? I thought you were a 
shoo-in for that position. 
Noel: So did I. Well, this morning, I made sure 
my resume was flawless and headed out the 
door in high spirits. 
Tori: That’s a good way to approach a job 
interview. 
Noel: I figured I had the job in the bag. I’ve got 
a solid background in nursing. My last employer 
gave me a great reference. Heck, I even 
graduated at the top of my nursing class. But 
was that enough to make the cut?  
Tori: You didn’t get the job, I take it. 
Noel: Bingo. An absolutely insufferable kid 
named Mitch interviewed me. He took one 
looking sharp = looking 
good; well-dressed 
why the long face? = why 
are you sad/upset? 
RN = registered nurse 
a shoo-in = a person who is 
certain to be selected 
flawless = perfect 
head out = leave (informal) 
in high spirits = happy, joyful 
had the job in the bag = 
would definitely get the job 
make the cut = be good 
enough to be accepted, 
according to a standard 
which will include some 
people and exclude others 
I take it = I assume; I guess 
or understand 
Bingo = (slang) you’re 
exactly right 
insufferable = impossible to 
tolerate 
Vocabulary 


 
 
glance at my resume, then tossed it aside. It 
seemed like he couldn’t care less about my 
experience. 
Tori: No way! So what did he ask you? 
Noel: Not much at all. Actually, he spent most of 
the interview rambling about the future of 
medical care. And every time I tried to bring up 
my strong points, he cut me off!   
Tori: I’ve had interviews with people like that… 
real know-it-alls who just want to put you 
down while making themselves look important 
and smart. They just like to hear themselves 
talk. 
Noel: According to him, I’m “not what Medical 
Alliance is looking for at the current time.” He 
said that they need bright and forward-
thinking nurses who can adapt to the ever-
changing medical world. 
Tori: And in his point of view, you didn’t fit the 
bill, huh? 
Noel: I really think he rejected me because of 
my gray hair! Look… I’m no spring chicken. 
But I know the ropes when it comes to nursing.  
took one glance = looked 
very briefly/quickly 
tossed it aside = casually put 
or threw it to the side 
couldn’t care less = 
completely didn’t care 
rambling = talking too long 
with too many details 
bring up = introduce a topic 
in conversation 
cut me off = interrupted me 
know-it-alls = people who 
think they are intellectually 
superior and know 
everything 
put you down = make you 
feel inferior 
bright = intelligent  
forward-thinking = describes 
someone innovative who 
thinks about the future 
didn’t fit the bill = not 
suitable for what is required 
no spring chicken = not a 
young person 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Tori: It seems like experience and qualifications 
aren’t enough anymore.  
Noel: Exactly. These young folks just see me as 
being out of date and out of touch with the 
modern world.  
Tori: I’m so sorry, Noel. The world is constantly 
changing…. people are changing. Times aren’t like 
they used to be.  
Noel: When I started out, all you needed to get 
your foot in the door were training and skills. But 
now it’s a whole new ball game. I have to try 
extra-hard to come across as innovative and 
dynamic. 
Tori: I know what you mean. I work in the music 
industry, and if I don’t keep up with the latest 
trends, I’ll get the axe in a heartbeat. Job security 
is a thing of the past. 
Noel: How am I even supposed to find a job when 
these stuck-up HR managers won’t hire perfectly 
capable nurses?  
Tori: Don’t lose heart, Noel – you’d be a great 
asset to any hospital. I’ll keep an eye out for any 
job opportunities.  
Noel: Thanks, Tori. I appreciate it. 
know the ropes = know 
an area well; know how to 
do something properly 
folks = people 
out of touch = not 
informed about current 
developments 
get your foot in the door 
= gain access/entry to an 
opportunity (especially a 
career) 
it’s a whole new ball 
game = it’s a completely 
different situation / set of 
circumstances 
come across as = make an 
impression of being a 
certain way 
get the axe = get fired, 
lose one’s job 
in a heartbeat = very fast, 
almost immediately 
Don’t lose heart = don’t 
become discouraged 
keep an eye out for = 
watch to see if something 
appears 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
a shoo-in 
fit the bill 
in high spirits 
lose heart 
a whole new ball game 
flawless 
keep an eye out 
make the cut 
bright 
I take it 
know the ropes 
out of touch 
couldn’t care less 
in a heartbeat 
know-it-all 
ramble 
 
1. Don't just ______________________ when you're on a first date - make sure to let 
the other person talk, too. 
2. Everyone was ______________________ on the day before summer vacation. 
3. He's refusing to answer my calls, so ______________________ he's still pretty angry 
at me. 
4. I just got hired at a bank, and I'm the least experienced person there - all my 
coworkers ______________________. 
5. That senator comes from a rich family; he's totally ______________________ with 
the working class. 
6. If I got the opportunity to move to Australia, I wouldn't hesitate - I'd go 
______________________. 
7. The gymnast's ______________________ performance was rewarded with a 10/10 
from the judges. 


 
 
8. My daughter is very ______________________. She's in first grade, but she's already 
reading at a third-grade level. 
9. We know the U.S. market very well, but doing business overseas is 
______________________. 
10. The holiday sale has ended, but make sure to ______________________ for future 
promotions! 
11. With an incredible 78% approval rating, the president is ______________________ 
for reelection. 
12. I needed a computer to do some heavy-duty video editing, and this model was 
the only one that ______________________. 
13. It's a terrible school because the teachers there ______________________ about the 
students. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
Speaking Task 
Describe, based on your observations, some changes you have seen over the course 
of your life. Talk about both changes in society and culture, and changes in your own 
personality or interests.  
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the MP3 to 
homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback and correction!

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 20: An Embarrassing Moment 
Jim and Fred are at a restaurant, and a waitress comes to take their order. Listen to 
what happens and mark these statements “True” or “False.” 
 
Listening Comprehension 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
1. Jim orders a bowl of clam chowder 
2. Fred orders one of today's specials 
3. Both of them want tap water to drink 
4. The waitress compliments Fred on his shirt 
5. Fred is attracted to the waitress 
6. It has been an easy week at work for Fred 
7. Fred has been wearing this shirt for years 
8. Fred bought the shirt himself 
9. The collar of the shirt is uncomfortable 
10. Fred becomes annoyed at Jim 
11. Fred asks for the waitress' phone number 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Waitress: Welcome to Rudy’s Diner! Our 
soup of the day is clam chowder, and our 
specials are Cajun chicken and barbecue 
ribs. What can I get for you guys? 
Jim: I’d like the steak – medium-rare – 
with a side of potatoes.  
Fred: And I’ll have the Cajun chicken, with 
extra hot sauce on the side.  
Waitress: All right, and anything to drink? 
Jim: Just tap water for me. 
Fred: A Diet Coke with no ice. 
Waitress: Coming right up! Nice shirt, by 
the way. 
 
Fred: Thank you!  
 
Jim: That IS a nice shirt, Fred. Very trendy. 
Fred: Thanks! You know, the waitress 
couldn’t take her eyes off me… and she’s 
pretty cute. You think I should ask for her 
number? 
Jim: Couldn’t hurt to try, when she comes 
back with the food. 
Fred: Yeah, okay. 
 
Jim: So… long day at work? 
clam chowder = a thick soup 
containing clams (a type of 
shellfish) in a milk or tomato 
base 
Cajun = a type of cooking from 
the New Orleans area, which is 
usually spicy 
barbecue ribs = “barbecue” 
refers to cooking meat over an 
open fire. “Ribs” are the bones 
and meat from the animal’s side, 
near its heart/lungs 
medium-rare = cooking the steak 
only until a point when it is still 
pink inside 
hot = spicy (it doesn’t refer to 
temperature here) 
tap water = regular water from 
the faucet (not bottled water) 
trendy = fashionable 
couldn’t take her eyes off me = 
continued to look at me 
couldn’t hurt to try = trying 
wouldn’t have any negative 
result 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Fred: Long week. I thought Friday would 
never come. 
Jim: Same here. Hey, back to your shirt… 
is it new? 
 
Fred: No, I’ve had it for years. First time 
I’ve worn it, though. Think I got it at a 
thrift shop… I dunno. 
 
Jim: Huh. ‘Cause I’ve never seen that STYLE 
of shirt before. 
 
Fred: Oh! Now I remember – it was a gift 
from my Aunt Kay. She’s got an eye for 
fashion. 
 
Jim: Yeah… I’d never thought of how cool 
buttons can look on the back of a shirt. 
 
Fred: Cool, but it makes the shirt hard to 
get into. I couldn’t reach the upper buttons, 
so I had to ask my roommate to give me a 
hand. 
 
Jim: I bet. And that collar. Man! It’s very… 
original.  
 
Fred: Yeah… I got a lot of compliments on 
it at work, but it’s kinda uncomfortable. 
Been tickling my neck all day. 
Jim: I guess that’s the price you pay for 
being a trend-setter, huh? Actually, your 
tag’s sticking out. Let me tuck that in for 
you. 
Same here = I feel the same way 
/ I’m in the same situation 
thrift shop = store that sells used 
clothing and items at low prices 
She’s got an eye for fashion = 
she has good taste / judgement 
regarding fashion 
give me a hand = help me 
(especially with a physical task) 
I bet = I’m completely sure 
collar = the part of the shirt 
around your neck 
original = new and creative, not 
like anything else 
tickling = touching lightly so that 
it’s uncomfortable or provokes 
laughter 
the price you pay = the 
consequences 
trend-setter = someone who 
establishes new fashions 
tuck in = put part of some 
fabric/clothing inside another 
part 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Fred: The tag? Oh, that’s why it’s been bothering 
me, it’s—hey, hold on a sec! 
 
Jim: Hahaha! 
 
Fred: Where’s the men’s room? I’ll be right back. 
 
Jim (when Fred returns to the table): Well, it took 
you long enough. Had to ask someone for help 
with the buttons?  
 
Fred: Why didn’t you just tell me?! I feel like an 
idiot. 
 
Jim: Where’s the fun in that? I wanted to keep 
dropping hints until you noticed.  
 
Fred: Some friend YOU are.  
 
Waitress: OK, here’s your steak and potatoes… 
and here’s your Cajun chicken. Hey! Your shirt 
looks much better that way. 
Fred: Uh, yeah. 
Waitress: Enjoy your meal, guys! 
 
Jim: Smooth… real smooth. Weren’t you going to 
ask for her number? I can call her back over and 
ask for some extra napkins… 
 
Fred: Forget it! As if she’d want to go out with 
some doofus who put his shirt on backwards. 
 
Jim: Aw man, that was the funniest thing that’s happened all week!  
 
Fred: Easy for you to say. I’ve never been more embarrassed in my life. 
hold on a sec! = wait a 
second! 
men's room = men’s 
bathroom 
an idiot = a stupid person 
dropping hints = 
suggesting indirectly 
Some friend YOU are = 
You’re not a very good 
friend (Fred is speaking 
sarcastically) 
smooth = (slang) well-
done, socially elegant (Jim 
is speaking sarcastically) 
doofus = (slang) 
incompetent person 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
bet 
give him a hand 
idiot 
tickling 
can't hurt 
got an eye for 
price we pay 
trendy 
couldn't take my eyes off 
hold on 
smooth 
tuck in 
dropping hints 
hot 
tap 
 
 
1. As we were leaving, Linda asked me to ____________________ while she changed 
her shoes. 
2. I made the baby laugh by tickling ____________________ stomach. 
3. That painting was absolutely gorgeous. I ____________________ it. 
4. I'm not sure if we're allowed to take pictures in the church, but it 
____________________ to ask. 
5. It takes us an hour to get to work, but that's the ____________________ for buying a 
house way outside the city. 
6. Nobody has natural muscles that big. I ____________________ he's on steroids. 
7. She hasn't broken up with her boyfriend yet, but she's been ____________________ 
that she's unhappy in the relationship. 
8. The chili is pretty ____________________; you'll definitely want a drink to wash it 
down. 
9. I saw an old man struggling with some heavy shopping bags, so I went over to 
____________________. 
10. The ____________________ water in this country isn't safe to use - not even for 
brushing your teeth. 
11. You should ask Brian to look over your design. He's ____________________ detail. 
12. The fire was caused by some ____________________ who tossed a lit cigarette into 
a garbage can filled with dry newspaper. 


 
 
Speaking Task 
Tell a funny story that has happened to you, or to a friend. It doesn’t necessarily 
have to be embarrassing, just amusing or interesting. Describe the situation in detail 
– record your story at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the MP3 to 
homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback!

1. False 
2. True

9. True 
10. True 
11. False

1. hold on 
2. tickling 
3. couldn't take my eyes off 
4. can't hurt 
5. price we pay 
6. bet 
7. dropping hints 
8. hot 
9. give him a hand

Lesson 21: Leadership 
Judy is struggling with her leadership role in a project, and Kevin gives her some 
suggestions. Listen to their conversation and mark these statements “True” or “False.” 
 
Listening Comprehension 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
1. Judy knew the project would be problematic from the beginning. 
2. The project is to improve the children's facilities at a library. 
3. Felix wants to modernize the selection of books. 
4. Cecily wants to use fewer shelves. 
5. The group agrees that the playground should be improved. 
6. Heidi wants to add more areas for different activities. 
7. Judy is the leader of the committee. 
8. The group has tried voting before, but it didn't work. 
9. Judy wants to get rid of all the extra plans. 
10. Kevin thinks Judy's idea of delegating is a good one. 
11. Judy has an upcoming meeting very soon. 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Judy: I thought this new project would be a piece 
of cake, but it’s turning out to be a real pain.  
 
Kevin: Sorry to hear that. What’s making it such a 
headache? 
 
Judy: The committee just can’t seem to agree on 
anything. Everyone has different ideas about 
what we should do; they’re all so stubborn, and 
I’m at my wits’ end! 
 
Kevin: OK, what’s the goal of your project? Fill 
me in on the details, and maybe I can help you 
out. 
 
Judy: We’re trying to improve the Children’s 
Center at the library. Just basic stuff like 
organizing and adding more shelves indoors, then 
renovating the playground outside.  
 
Kevin: Seems pretty simple. So what’s the issue? 
 
Judy: Basically, Felix wants to sort through the 
old books before we start adding more shelves; 
he says the books are outdated. Then Cecily 
insists that we need to return the shelves we 
already bought and get new, safer ones instead. 
Everyone’s keen on improving the playground, 
but half the people say they have back problems 
so they won’t be able to help. And the ones that 
can work on the playground are bickering about 
which materials we should use.

a real pain / a headache = 
very annoying 
stubborn = describes a 
person who is convinced 
they are right, and doesn’t 
change their mind easily 
I’m at my wits’ end = at 
the limit of your mental 
resources, desperate and 
without additional options 
fill me in on = give 
someone information they 
are lacking 
renovating = repair and 
improve a building or 
structure 
sort through = go through 
a collection and organize 
or classify the items 
outdated = old-fashioned; 
not modern 
keen on = excited about 
bickering = arguing (often 
over insignificant things) 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Kevin: I see…. 
 
Judy: Laura and Ned want to do a pizza 
fundraiser to get more money for the project. 
They want to expand the playground to 
include a skateboard area and a climbing wall. 
But Heidi thinks we should use the extra 
money to improve the handicapped ramps 
on the playground and maybe even add a 
wheelchair lift near the entrance.  
 
Kevin: It sounds like your group is great at 
brainstorming, but if you can’t come to a 
consensus, then you’ll be doing nothing more 
than spinning your wheels.  
 
Judy: You nailed it. At every meeting, we get 
so bogged down in discussion that nothing 
gets done. I’m supposed to be the leader, but 
if I put my foot down and make the 
decisions, some people are always going to be 
upset. 
 
Kevin: Well, you can’t please everyone. But 
the group does have to agree in advance that 
whatever decisions are made, everybody will 
uphold them. Do you have a voting process? 
 
Judy: No… for some reason, we haven’t 
thought about voting on things. It’s just been a 
lot of talking and arguing for hours on end. 
 
Kevin: Voting is great because everyone can 
voice their ideas, but then the majority 
decides on what the group does – and since

getting monetary donations 
for a project or cause 
handicapped = refers to 
people with disabilities 
ramps = inclined areas 
brainstorming = creating 
many new ideas 
consensus = agreement 
spinning your wheels = 
wasting time staying in the 
same position, not advancing 
You nailed it = you’re exactly 
right 
bogged down = stuck, slow, 
unable to progress 
put my foot down = take a 
firm position 
uphold = support 
hours on end = many 
consecutive hours

Vocabulary 


 
 
everyone’s vote is equal, nobody can accuse 
you of favoritism.  
Judy: That’s a good idea. Got any other tips for 
me? 
 
Kevin: Another one is to make a clear 
distinction between what NEEDS to be done 
and what people WANT to do. This will help 
keep the group focused.   
 
Judy: I like that. But what should we do about 
all the extra plans? There are some good ones 
in there, and I don’t want people feeling like 
their ideas are always shot down. 
 
Kevin: There are a couple different ways you 
could deal with it. You could always vote on the 
extras and have the group pick the best one. 
Another way is to divide the project into “Phase 
1” – doing only what’s essential to the goal – 
and then “Phase 2” – adding extra stuff later. 
Judy: Hey, and I just thought of something else 
– the people who are suggesting the extra stuff, 
I could empower them to head up those 
projects. That way it wouldn’t all be on my 
shoulders. 
Kevin: Now you’re catching on. Remember 
that leading a group of people is definitely a 
learning process. Let me know how your next 
meeting goes. 
Judy: Speaking of which, I gotta get ready 
because it starts in an hour! Thanks, Kevin. 
You’ve given me a lot of food for thought.

means it criticized and 
rejected

Lesson 22: Ethical Marketing 
Mitch and Brent are business partners who work in advertising; they are debating 
whether to take on a particular project. Listen and answer the following questions: 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Mitch wants to take the job because... 
a. he'll make a lot of money 
b. it's an intriguing project 
c. the company will give him free products 
2. The product is... 
a. a medicine 
b. a vitamin 
c. an energy drink 
3. Why is Brent hesitant to advertise the product? 
a. its claims are exaggerated 
b. it hasn't been approved by the government 
c. it could make teenagers addicted 
4. Mitch says if they don't accept the project... 
a. their reputation will be ruined 
b. they won't have enough money to pay the bills 
c. the client will work with a different advertiser 
5. Brent is concerned about him and Mitch... 
a. facing legal trouble 
b. getting sick 
c. having to lie  
6. Mitch proposes... 
a. adjusting the ads' messaging 
b. partnering with another ad agency 
c. waiting until the product is more popular 
7. At the end, they decide... 
a. to accept the client 
b. not to accept the client 
c. to re-negotiate the contract 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Mitch: We’ve gotta think of a clever 
slogan. If this client likes our stuff, we’ll be 
rolling in dough.  
Brent: Whoa, hold your horses. Let’s take 
it one step at a time. You know, I’ve been 
having second thoughts about whether 
we should even take on this job.  
Mitch: What?! Come on, Brent, this is the 
top supplement company in the world! It’s 
our chance to break into the big leagues. 
Brent: But the product in question is kinda 
dubious. A very controversial new energy 
drink that hasn’t been approved by the 
Food and Drug Administration… I’m not 
sure I can market that in good conscience. 
Mitch: These energy drinks are all the 
rage nowadays! If we come up with a 
killer advertisement targeted towards 
teens, these drinks will be flying off the 
shelves. 
Brent: Yeah, it’s just that this product is 
still in a trial stage. If anything goes wrong, 
slogan = short, memorable phrase 
used in advertising 
rolling in dough = (slang) having a 
LOT of money 
hold your horses = (informal) 
wait; don’t be so quick to take 
action 
having second thoughts = 
reconsidering, doubting a 
previous decision 
the big leagues = a high level of 
activity or competition 
dubious = questionable, subject 
to doubts 
in good conscience = without 
feeling guilty 
all the rage = extremely popular 
come up with = create 
killer = (slang) excellent 
flying off the shelves = selling 
very fast 
Vocabulary 


 
 
it could be a catastrophe for the company – 
and for us, too. But once the FDA okays it, then 
sure – we can go for it. 
Mitch: You wanna wait for the FDA? Don’t 
hold your breath. They take forever to 
approve a product, and by the time they do, our 
client will have found a new advertising team. 
We will have missed the boat.  
Brent: Missing the boat is better than being 
smacked with a lawsuit if people start getting 
sick from this energy drink. I’m not about to 
risk my neck for ten pounds of sugar, caffeine, 
and who knows what else crammed into a tiny 
bottle.  
Mitch: What are the odds of us getting sued, 
though? People will go after the manufacturer, 
not the advertiser. You’re being too cautious. 
Brent: And you’re being too reckless. Not only 
could we end up losing money on lawsuits, but 
we’d also lose our reputation – and that’s not so 
easy to recover from. 
Mitch: What if we take on the client, but tone 
down the messaging of the ads? And of course 
we’d have a disclaimer that the energy drink 
isn’t FDA approved. 
catastrophe = very big 
disaster 
okays = (informal) approves 
Don’t hold your breath = 
don’t wait for it, because it 
will never happen 
missed the boat = missed the 
opportunity 
being smacked with a lawsuit 
= getting hit with legal action 
against you 
risk my neck = take a risk that 
could result in a very serious 
disaster 
crammed = put into a small 
space 
What are the odds = what are 
the chances 
reckless = being irresponsible; 
acting without being careful 
tone down = make less 
intense, less shocking 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Brent: I dunno, I’ve just got a gut feeling that 
this one’s a bad bet. Plus, we’ve got no 
shortage of clients. Let’s make our millions 
with a product we can actually be proud of.  
Mitch: Okay... if you’re not sold on this project, 
then we’ll have to turn it down. It would be too 
much work for me to take on solo. ::sigh::  So 
much for our big break. 
Brent: I’m sure another great opportunity will 
come along. And look on the bright side… at 
least we’ll be able to sleep better at night. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
got a gut feeling = have a 
feeling of certainty that is 
deep and hard to explain 
rationally  
a bad bet = a potential 
project that is likely to have 
bad results/consequences 
no shortage of = no lack of (in 
other words, they have a lot 
of other clients) 
not sold on = not convinced 
of the value of 
solo = (informal) alone 
So much for = this is the end 
of; this will not happen 
big break = a fortunate 
moment when you become 
famous or successful 
look on the bright side = 
consider the positive aspects 
sleep better at night = be 
calm and not feel anxious or 
agitated 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz

1. Don't tell me you're having ______________________ about moving to Atlanta. We've 
already bought a house there, we can't back out now! 
2. He probably would have won the scholarship, but he didn't apply in time, so he 
______________________. 
3. I couldn't resist ordering the chocolate fudge cake for dessert... 
______________________ my diet. 
4. Sorry, but I'm ______________________ the need for such an advanced camera. The 
basic model will do just fine. 
5. It's a very simple, safe operation. The ______________________ of any complications 
are next to nothing. 
6. Our first attempt at starting a business was a ______________________; we lost our 
life savings. 
7. She's still as ______________________ as ever - she was just caught driving drunk for 
the third time this year. 
8. Skinny jeans are ______________________; I see people wearing them everywhere. 
9. I can't take credit for that idea. Jerry was the one who ______________________ it. 
10. The duo played at small local venues for years before their ______________________. 
Now they're touring internationally. 
11. There were fifty people ______________________ into a classroom designed to seat 
twenty. 
12. I just went shopping, so there's ______________________ food in the house. 


 
 
Speaking Task 
There are two options for today’s speaking task, so you can choose one to answer: 
a. Have you ever faced an ethical dilemma, when you weren’t sure about the right 
thing to do? Describe the situation and how you decided to handle it. 
b. Do you believe “right” and “wrong” are absolute certainties, or do they depend 
on the context? Give an example to support your opinion. 
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the MP3 to 
homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback!

Lesson 23: Getting a Raise 
Vance and Aaron are co-workers who have the same boss, Mr. Brown. Listen to Aaron 
give Vance advice on getting a raise, and answer these comprehension questions: 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Vance wants a raise because... 
a. he wants to go on vacation 
b. he's going to get married 
c. his wife wants to buy a house 
2. He's been working for the company for... 
a. ten years 
b. twelve years 
c. twenty years 
3. Mr. Brown can best be described as... 
a. arrogant 
b. perfectionistic 
c. strict 
4. How does Aaron recommend approaching Mr. Brown? 
a. by giving him lots of compliments 
b. carefully and indirectly 
c. with clarity and confidence 
5. Aaron asked for a raise because... 
a. another company offered him a better salary 
b. his kids were going into university 
c. he had worked there longer than anyone else 
6. Vance is especially worried about getting fired because... 
a. he has a lot of student loans to pay off 
b. he'll have difficulty getting another job 
c. his wife is going to have a baby 
7. What does he decide to do at the end of the dialogue? 
a. invite Mr. Brown to his house 
b. talk to Mr. Brown today 
c. send Mr. Brown an e-mail 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Vance: I really, really, need a raise. Melinda 
isn’t saying it to my face, but she wants this 
house we looked at on Snowy Lane. She knows 
we can’t afford it unless I get a raise. 
Aaron: So talk to Mr. Brown and ask for one. 
You’ve been with this company for a decade 
now, and you’ve got a great track record. 
You’re honest. You put in overtime when 
needed. You deserve a raise. 
Vance: I know, I know. It’s just that Mr. Brown 
is always fussing about how we need to cut 
costs around here. He’s not exactly the type of 
boss that hands out raises like candy. 
Aaron: Mr. Brown definitely doesn’t tolerate 
any nonsense. But sometimes that’s for the 
best.  
Vance: How so? 
Aaron: Mr. Brown respects men who are 
upfront and straightforward. He doesn’t like 
weaklings. If you go into his office hanging 
your head and beating around the bush he’s 
just gonna kick you out.  
saying it to my face = saying it 
directly to me 
can’t afford = won’t have 
enough money to buy 
a great track record = a great 
history of performance 
overtime = working more 
than normal hours 
fussing = complaining 
upfront = direct 
weakling = an informal word 
for someone who is weak 
hanging your head = having 
your head down, as if 
ashamed 
beating around the bush = 
saying words that are 
somewhat related, but not 
saying the main point 
kick you out = expel, put you 
out by force 
march = walk confidently 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
You have to march into that man’s office with your 
chin up, look him in the eye, and ask with 
confidence. That’s what I did. 
Vance: And Mr. Brown gave you a raise? 
Aaron: Not right away. At first he yelled at me and 
then he threw a lot of financial numbers around 
and so on. But I held my ground. My twins were 
about to go to college, with a double tuition bill to 
boot. So I let him know that unless I got a raise I 
would have to leave and find a job that would 
support my family better. 
Vance: I can’t believe you pulled that off. 
Aaron: Look, Mr. Brown isn’t blind. He knows the 
cost of living is going up. He also knows we give it 
our all. If you go in there asking for a raise to buy 
a new boat, then you don’t have a chance. But if 
you explain that you want to buy a new home for 
your pregnant wife, I’m sure he’ll understand.  
Vance: The apartment Melinda and I are living in 
is pretty small – and when the baby arrives, space 
will be very tight. 
Aaron: Then march into Mr. Brown’s office and 
tell him just that. I promise you, he’s a reasonable 
man. Sure he might bark at you, but don’t back 
down.  
and so on = and more of 
this type of thing 
I held my ground = I 
maintained my position 
and didn’t give up 
to boot = informal way to 
say “in addition” 
pulled that off = managed 
to succeed in doing 
something difficult 
isn’t blind = is not 
unaware of what’s 
happening 
give it our all = give our 
best effort and energy 
tight = in this context it 
means small and 
uncomfortable 
bark at = speak harshly to 
someone 
don’t back down = don’t 
change your position or 
belief 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vance: Hope I don’t catch him on a bad day. I can just 
picture getting fired with a baby on the way. 
Aaron: You’re not going to get fired. Now go see Mr. 
Brown before he leaves for the day. 
Vance: Well… here goes. Raise or no raise, I have to 
try. Melinda – and the baby – deserve it. 
Aaron: That’s the spirit! And don’t be surprised if Mr. 
Brown melts a little and buys you a housewarming 
present.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
picture = imagine 
here goes = an 
expression when the 
speaker is about to 
perform a bold, risky, 
or difficult action 
melts = in this 
context, it refers to 
becoming less “hard” 
and showing more 
emotion 
a housewarming 
present = a gift to 
celebrate moving into 
a new house 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz

give it your all

to boot

picturing

blind

classes and excelled in none.

4. My manager has a hard time giving criticism; she prefers to ____________________

11. You shouldn't expect to succeed if you're not willing to ____________________.

Lesson 24: Language Learning 
Pat is getting married, and he’s determined to learn his future wife’s native language. 
He talks with John about his difficulties. Listen and answer these ten questions: 
Comprehension Questions 
1. Pat is learning how to speak... 
a. German 
b. Italian 
c. Russian 
2. How long until his wedding? 
a. six days 
b. six weeks 
c. six months 
3. John advises him to... 
a. focus on the basics 
b. get a private tutor 
c. try a software program 
4. Pat wants to learn... 
a. because he promised he would 
b. so he can live in another country 
c. to surprise Veronica 
5. What language did John learn? 
a. French 
b. Irish 
c. Spanish 
 


 
 
6. John's biggest challenge was... 
a. grammar 
b. pronunciation 
c. vocabulary 
7. How is Veronica's English? 
a. basic 
b. decent 
c. fluent 
8. Pat is especially worried about... 
a. having Veronica laugh at him 
b. saying his wedding vows 
c. making small talk with Veronica’s relatives 
9. He's also doubting... 
a. the idea of getting married 
b. whether he should have a bilingual wedding 
c. whether or not Veronica loves him 
10. 
At the end of the conversation, he decides to... 
a. admit to Veronica that he can't do it 
b. ask his mother-in-law for help 
c. keep studying and try his best 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Pat: How can I learn to speak Russian when I can’t 
even understand how to read it? And the wedding is 
just six months away. There’s no way, John… there’s 
just no way I can learn to speak Russian before then.  
John: You’re the one who’s marrying a Russian bride. 
But hey, chill out, Pat. The important thing is that you 
learn the basics. No one can really learn a language 
fluently in six months… not that I know of, at least. 
Pat: I know, but Veronica and I promised each other 
that we would learn each other’s language before our 
wedding. English isn’t exactly rocket science… but 
Russian sure seems like it. 
John: Hey, don’t knock the English language. How do 
you know Veronica isn’t having the same worries you 
are? I remember when I took classes to learn French… 
I wanted to learn the “romantic” language to sweep 
Tori off her feet. 
Pat: Yeah, I remember. You’re pretty fluent now, 
aren’t you?  
John: Yeah, but not at first. Pat, we’re from Georgia. 
When I first started to learn French I sounded like a 
drunken French hillbilly.

isn’t rocket science = 
isn’t extremely difficult 
don’t knock = don’t 
make fun of, don’t 
insult

= make her fall in love 
with me very quickly 
drunken = when you 
have consumed too 
much alcohol. We can 
also say a person is 
drunk. 
hillbilly = someone 
from the countryside, 
from a less developed 
part of the country 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Not only did I have to learn the ins and outs of the 
language, I had to get the hang of the accent. Tori 
couldn’t stop laughing the first time I spoke French 
to her. 
Pat: You seem to be doing okay now, though.  
John: And all it took was five years of forcing my 
mouth to get rid of my southern drawl and try to 
sound like a French aristocrat.  
Pat: I don’t have five years… and now that you 
mention it, I didn’t even think about my accent. Oh 
man, I’m gonna sound like a Russian hillbilly.  
John: No you won’t. You were raised in the capital. 
My point is that learning a new language takes time. 
I bet you ten bucks Veronica will not be speaking 
fluent English by the time of your wedding. And 
she’s got a thick Russian accent.  
Pat: Maybe so, John, but at least she already speaks 
decent English. I can’t even say hello in Russian yet. 
I can just see us saying our vows… I’m supposed to 
say mine in Russian and Veronica is supposed to 
say hers in English. What if I mess up and swear 
my eternal love to her left shoe or something? 
John: You will not, now stop it. Listen to me. You’re 
a pretty smart fella. The only mistake you’re 
making is allowing a new language to intimidate

tiny details

by practicing

accent from the southern 
part of the U.S. is often 
called a “drawl” – a slow 
way of speaking that 
prolongs the words

accent

Vocabulary 


 
 
you.  I admit the Russian language isn’t a piece of 
cake, but surely you can make a dent in it.  
Pat: I know…I know…maybe I’m just worried about 
the wedding, you know… being a married man and 
all. I love Veronica, but the thought of a life-long 
commitment… 
John: You’ll be just fine. And if you do love 
Veronica—which you just admitted—then you’ll 
learn the Russian language for her sake. Or at least 
– so you can argue with your mother-in-law! 
Pat: Argh, don’t remind me! It’s true, though – 
there’s nothing in the world that I wouldn’t do for 
Veronica.  
John: So man up and start studying! 
Pat: All right – here, help quiz me on these 
flashcards so I don’t make a fool of myself!

2. Do you think it's better for unhappy couples to divorce, or to stay together

3. He looks like he's about to explode; when I told him to _______________________ he 
nearly bit my head off. 
4. I wanted to show off my new dance moves, but instead I tripped and fell and

Lesson 25: An Inspiring Teacher 
High-school students Nate and Ralph are talking about Mr. Smith, their favorite teacher. 
Listen to their conversation and answer these comprehension questions: 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Which subject does Mr. Smith teach? 
a. biology 
b. chemistry 
c. psychology 
2. Nate only passed the final because Mr. Smith... 
a. let him have extra time to finish 
b. tutored him before the exam 
c. was generous in his grading 
3. Ralph says that Mr. Smith's classes are... 
a. challenging 
b. easy 
c. fun 
4. Mr. Smith has been teaching for... 
a. 29 years 
b. 45 years 
c. 74 years 
5. If Nate hadn't passed the test, he would likely have to... 
a. go to an inferior college 
b. join the military 
c. work for his father 
6. What does Nate suggest doing for Mr. Smith? 
a. buying him a nice gift 
b. having a party 
c. writing a letter of appreciation 
7. Ralph suggests... 
a. nominating Mr. Smith for an award 
b. staying in touch with Mr. Smith 
c. taking another class with Mr. Smith next year 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Ralph: I thought I was going to flunk 
chemistry for sure. 
Nate: Ditto. I just barely squeaked by with a 
66 on the final. The saving grace was that Mr. 
Smith gave me partial credit for a few of the 
answers.  
Ralph: Mr. Smith is awesome. He really cares 
about his students. I can’t say the same about 
most of our teachers. 
Nate: I’m just thanking my lucky stars that I 
had Mr. Smith for chemistry, and not Ms. 
Johnson. She’s a stickler for perfection. 
Ralph: Or Mr. Potter. He just drones on 
without a break. But Mr. Smith always tries to 
spice things up with a joke or a game during 
class. 
Nate: Let me tell you, when I got my final 
grades, I breathed a huge sigh of relief. If I’d 
failed that exam, I could have lost my 
scholarship. But I didn’t, thanks to Mr. Smith. 
Ralph: And I was completely fed up with 
chemistry and ready to drop the class, but he 
went out of his way to help and encourage me.  
flunk = fail (slang) 
Ditto = me too (slang) 
squeaked by = barely manage 
to win, pass, or survive 
something 
I can’t say the same about = 
in other cases it’s different 
thanking my lucky stars = 
extremely grateful for good 
fortune 
a stickler = someone who 
insists on something and is 
not flexible 
drones on = speaks 
continuously in a monotone 
voice 
spice things up = make things 
more interesting, exciting, or 
fun 
breathed a huge sigh of relief 
= was extremely relieved in 
that moment 
fed up with = not willing to 
endure any longer 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Nate: Did you know that he’s seventy-four years old? 
Ralph: No way! Mr. Smith can’t be that old. 
Nate: He told me he started teaching when he was 29, 
and he’s been doing it for 45 years – so, do the math. 
Just think how many students he’s helped over the 
years. How many lives he’s changed. 
Ralph: Yours, for one. If you’d lost your scholarship, 
you’d probably end up working in your dad’s 
furniture factory. 
Nate: That’s a dead-end job. I don’t even wanna 
think about it! 
Ralph: And if I’d failed, I would’ve gotten an earful 
from my mom. Plus we’d both have to make up the 
credit in summer school.  
Nate: Hey… why don’t we do something nice for Mr. 
Smith? You know, to give him props for being such a 
great teacher.  
Ralph: What do you have in mind? 
Nate: Well, we can get the gang together and throw a 
surprise party. We’ll sneak into school early Friday 
morning and set it up in the classroom.  
Ralph: Sounds cool. We can also invite the other 
teachers. I’m sure they all have a soft spot for Mr. 
Smith; he’s been at this school practically forever.

made a special effort 
beyond normal 
responsibility 
do the math = figure 
out the answer by 
yourself 
dead-end job = a job 
with no possibility of 
advancement 
gotten an earful from 
my mom = have to 
listen to a lot of 
criticism or lecturing

needed

friends (informal)

have a bit of special 
affection for 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Nate: I can’t believe our graduation is just around 
the corner. Soon Mr. Smith and everyone else in 
this place will be a distant memory. 
Ralph: I’ll really miss walking into his classroom 
and listening to him tell his corny jokes.  
Nate: With that goofy bowtie he always wears. Aw 
man, now I’ve got a lump in my throat.  
Ralph: I wonder if Mr. Smith keeps tabs on his old 
students? You know, through Facebook or 
something. We’ll have to look him up. 
Nate: Yeah. Come on, let’s go plan that party.

over time

1. Glad to hear you got a ticket! I ___________________________ - they were all sold out 
by the time I tried to buy one. 
2. I thought I'd left my front door unlocked; I ___________________________ when I got 
home and found that I hadn't. 
3. We're completely ___________________________ the terrible customer service from 
our internet provider, so we're going to switch. 
4. Karen has really improved things in this department. I'd like to 
___________________________ for all the great work she's done. 
5. My friend ___________________________ his wife when she found flirty texts from 
another woman on his phone. 
6. The librarian ___________________________ to help me find every single book I 
needed for my research. 
7. I'm involved in so many projects that I need an assistant just to help me 
___________________________  everything. 
8. There's no way I'm wearing that ___________________________ giant green hat. 
9. My editor says the middle part of the book is kind of boring; she wants me to 
add more action to ___________________________. 
10. When I got a flat tire in the middle of the night, I ___________________________ that 
my dad had taught me how to change a tire. 
11. Your 30th wedding anniversary is ___________________________! Do you have any 
special plans? 
12. The whole team played terribly. Their ___________________________ was that the 
goalkeeper managed to keep the ball out of the net.

Talk about someone who has inspired you and had a major influence on your life. It 
can be someone who you know personally, or someone who you don’t know but you

send the MP3 to homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback!

Lesson 26: A Great Vacation 
 
Kate has just returned from vacation, and Julia asks her about it. Listen and answer 
the comprehension questions: 
 
1. Kate went to... 
a. the Netherlands 
b. Norway 
c. New Zealand 
2. She went in the... 
a. summer 
b. fall 
c. winter 
3. She highlights the beauty of the... 
a. architecture 
b. culture 
c. scenery 
4. One disadvantage was... 
a. it was expensive 
b. she had no friends there 
c. the food wasn't good 
5. Julia can't travel as much because of her... 
a. children 
b. job 
c. studies 
6. She will travel next year because... 
a. she's going to a conference 
b. she's getting married 
c. she's studying abroad 
7. Kate says that Paris is lovely because it's... 
a. inexpensive 
b. old-fashioned 
c. peaceful 
8. Which place does she recommend for its people? 
a. Greece 
 
b. Ireland 
 
c. Italy 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Julia: Hey Kate, welcome back! How was your 
vacation? 
 
Kate: It was wonderful! Norway is an amazing 
place. I saw some breathtaking scenery and I 
feel like I got to recharge my batteries. 
 
Julia: How was the weather? 
 
Kate: There’s a Norwegian expression: We 
don’t have summer, just two months of 
crummy ski conditions. So even though it was 
June, it was chilly. We were all bundled up in 
fleeces and winter hats.  
 
Julia: Haha, and meanwhile here we’ve been 
having a heat wave! What was the country 
like? 
 
Kate: Oh, the spectacular countryside more 
than made up for the cool weather. Norway 
has the rolling hills of Ireland and the snow-
capped mountains of the Canadian Rockies. 
We explored these little water inlets where 
you could spot at least one waterfall from 
anywhere you stood.  
 
Julia: That sounds incredible. How’d it stack 
up against all the other places you’ve been? 
 
Kate: Well, it was the most expensive city in 
Europe I’ve been to, so that’s one downside. 
We splurged on a nice hotel, so we didn’t

that are amazingly beautiful

and recover my energy

(click here for a picture)

have much left over for food. Basically we ate

the city that I could crash with. 
 
Julia: You’re lucky you can just take off and travel 
whenever the impulse strikes. I wish I could 
travel more, but my boss doesn’t let me take much 
time off… she says I’m indispensable. I’m not 
sure if that’s a blessing or a curse! 
 
Kate: But you do have your honeymoon next

Julia: Um, our plans are still up in the air. 
Actually, I’d love to hear your take. Of all the 
places you’ve been, which one do you recommend 
most? 
 
Kate: That’s a really tough question. It all hinges 
on what you’re looking for. If you want classy 
architecture in a romantic city, definitely go to 
Paris. It’s well-preserved because France was 
quick to surrender during World War II, so it’s 
like you’re visiting a different time period. A lot of 
other cities still have old buildings of course, but 
they’re mixed in with modern skyscrapers as 
well. 
 
Julia: Good to know. Do you have any other 
pointers? 
 
Kate: If you want a more traditional honeymoon 
atmosphere in a warm climate, try the Greek 
islands. All the villages are built into the rocky 
cliff face, and the houses are white, which is a

outgoing people, check out Italy. And if you’re 
looking for a quaint bed-and-breakfast type place 
in the countryside, I’d recommend Ireland.  
 
Julia: I’ve gotta jot this down! All these places 
sound great, it seems impossible to choose just

Kate: Why not quit your job? Then you’d have all 
the time in the world to travel. 
 
Julia: Sure. But then I couldn’t afford to go

Lesson 27: Bad Habits 
Mandy wants her boyfriend, Toby, to get rid of some bad habits. Listen to their 
conversation and try to answer these comprehension questions: 
1. Toby's bad habit is... 
a. biting his nails 
b. chewing on toothpicks 
c. picking his nose 
2. Mandy's bad habit is... 
a. cracking her knuckles 
b. chewing her lip 
c. playing with her hair 
3. Mandy wants him to stop because... 
a. he's going on a job interview 
b. her friends are coming to visit 
c. she wants to introduce Toby to her parents 
4. Toby works as a... 
a. construction worker 
b. farmer 
c. veterinarian 
5. Toby also makes a remark about Mandy's... 
a. eating habits 
b. hobbies 
c. whiny voice 
6. Toby says that his bad habit... 
a. has been with him since childhood 
b. is something practically everyone does 
c. isn't so bad when compared to others 
7. Toby suggests... 
a. making a deal to ignore each other's bad habits 
b. replacing their bad habits with conversation 
c. that bad habits are necessary to deal with stress. 
8. Mandy also wants to change Toby's... 
a. clothing 
 
b. haircut 
 
c. way of speaking 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
Mandy: Will you stop biting your fingernails? It’s 
so gross. 
Toby: Hey, Valley Girl, this is Texas, not Los 
Angeles. Here in Texas a guy can bite his nails. 
Mandy: I’m not asking you to get a manicure – I 
just want my boyfriend to have decent-looking 
hands. Your fingernails have these ragged edges… 
they look like they’ve been gnawed on by a 
rodent.  
Toby: Doesn’t bother me. Besides, hands were 
made for workin’. Heck, ain’t no cow looking at my 
fingernails when I’m doing the milking. 
Mandy: We’re not on your farm, Toby, so get with 
the program. Next week my friends from LA are 
driving here to see me. If they see your nasty 
fingernails they’ll think you’re a slob. Like, for 
sure. 
Toby: Look, I’m a farmer, and darn proud of it. And 
if I want to bite my fingernails I will. It’s not like I 
chew my bottom lip like you do. 
Mandy: What’s that supposed to mean? 
Toby: Oh, come down off your high horse. You’re 
always biting your bottom lip like it’s a juicy steak 
or something. What’s the matter, the celery stick 
you ate for breakfast wasn’t enough for you? 
Mandy: Hey – I don’t wanna hear any of your snide 
comments about my weight! 
gross = disgusting 
manicure = get your nails 
professionally cleaned and 
decorated 
ragged edges = the edges of 
his nails are uneven, as 
though they were torn 
gnawed on = chewed 
rodent = rat or other similar 
animal 
ain’t = (informal) there isn’t 
get with the program = 
follow the rules, do what 
you’re supposed to do 
nasty = disgusting 
a slob = a dirty, messy 
person who doesn’t take 
care of themselves 
come down off your high 
horse = don’t act so 
superior 
juicy steak = piece of 
meat that’s full of liquid 
snide = sarcastic, insulting 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Toby: All I’m saying is that you’ve got your 
vices too – so don’t fuss about mine. 
Mandy: You’re hopeless. Biting your nails 
is, like, a habit most people grow out of by 
the time they’re ten. It’s about time you 
stopped. 
Toby: It’s about time you stopped chewing 
on your lip. You’re doing it right now!  
Mandy: Okay! Fine – it’s a bad habit. But so 
is biting your nails.  
Toby: Yeah, but there are a lot of worse 
ones – like cussing and chewing tobacco 
and hitting the bottle, like my old man 
does. But I don’t do any of those. I just bite 
my fingernails when I get aggravated or 
stressed, that’s all.  
Mandy: That’s the same reason I chew on 
my lower lip. I don’t even realize I’m doing 
it. 
Toby: Okay, fine, then let’s make a deal. 
Whenever we feel the need to bite a 
fingernail or chew on a lip, we’ll just talk to 
each other instead. Deal? 
Mandy: Deal. I knew there was a reason I 
liked you. But you still need a makeover, 
farmer boy. I’ll never hear the end of it if 
my friends see you in those grubby 
overalls… 
Toby: Oh good grief, here we go again.  
 
vices = terrible habit or addiction 
fuss = worry and complain 
You’re hopeless = there’s no hope or 
possibility of you changing or 
improving 
grow out of = stop doing as you grow 
up and become more mature 
It’s about time = this should have 
happened a long time ago 
cussing = swearing, using bad 
language 
hitting the bottle = (slang) 
drinking alcohol 
my old man = (slang) my father 
aggravated = very annoyed 
makeover = complete 
change/improvement of your 
appearance 
I’ll never hear the end of it = I’ll 
constantly be reminded of by 
someone 
grubby = worn-out and dirty 
overalls = a type of pants with 
straps that go over the shoulders, 
often worn by farmers (picture) 
Vocabulary

learn not to do it in public! 
2. My best friend roots for a rival sports team. If they win the championship this

3. He used to be a light drinker, but he started ______________________  more

9. This T-shirt is a bit ______________________, so I wear it for doing housework and 
things like that. 
10. You've dropped three classes and are failing two more! If you don't 
______________________, you won't graduate on time. 
11. Christina got a ______________________ before her 21st birthday - she bought new 
clothes and completely changed her hairstyle and color. 
12. These shoes have tooth marks in them because our new puppy was 
______________________  them.

Lesson 28: Wealth and Poverty 
 
Two friends, Janet and Elise, discuss the political views of Elise’s husband. Mark these 
statements “True” or “False” as you listen. 
 
Listening Comprehension 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
 
1. Elise wasn't really aware of her husband's views when they were dating. 
2. Janet implies that Elise should divorce her husband. 
3. Nowadays, Elise and her husband have angry arguments about politics. 
4. Republicans want to take money from the rich and give it to the poor. 
5. Michael is prejudiced against poor people. 
6. Elise admits she doesn't know a lot about economics. 
7. Janet's profession involves social work. 
8. Elise is just as worried as Janet about Michael's political orientation. 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Janet: I can’t believe your husband is a 
Republican. Didn’t you know that when 
you tied the knot? 
 
Elise: When we were dating, he was 
always pretty tight-lipped about his 
political views… he described himself as a 
moderate. And whenever he brought up 
points that countered my opinions, I 
figured he was just playing devil’s 
advocate.  
 
Janet: He misled you, though. I mean, 
every relationship has its ups and downs, 
but that’s a serious breach of trust. Don’t 
tell me you’re going to stick with him! 
 
Elise: Look, some of his comments do rub 
me the wrong way, but it’s not like we’re 
at each other’s throats about these 
issues. You’ve gotta pick your battles, 
and I’m not about to end my marriage just 
because we don’t see eye to eye on some 
things. 
tied the knot = (informal) got 
married 
 
tight-lipped = reluctant to speak 
 
playing devil’s advocate = arguing 
from the point of view of the 
opposite side just to generate 
discussion 
 
misled = influenced you to 
believe something that wasn’t 
true 
 
ups and downs = good times and 
bad times 
 
breach = break (especially of an 
agreement) 
 
stick with him = stay with him 
 
rub me the wrong way = 
irritate/annoy me a little 
 
at each other’s throats = in an 
angry disagreement 
 
pick your battles = choose which 
things you are willing to fight for, 
and which you are willing to 
tolerate 
 
don’t see eye to eye  
= don’t agree 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Janet: But doesn’t it make you think less of 
his character? Republicans are selfish and 
stingy. 
 
Elise: How can you make a blanket 
statement like that? You know Michael, he’s 
a kind and generous man.  
 
Janet: Just look at the Republican stance on 
economics, for instance. They favor the rich 
and think the poor should just pull 
themselves up by their bootstraps. 
 
Elise: I don’t think it’s quite that simple. 
Granted, I don’t eat, sleep, and breathe 
politics like you do, but… 
 
Janet: Let me break it down for you. 
Republicans want tax breaks for the 
wealthy. The rationale is that rich people 
will spend more money and stimulate the 
economy for everybody. But the distribution 
of wealth in this country is already so 
lopsided, how can anyone argue that 
helping the rich stay rich will solve the 
problem? 
 
stingy = the opposite of 
generous, someone who is not 
willing to give to help others 
 
make a blanket statement = 
generalize; make a statement 
about an entire group of people 
 
stance = position, opinion 
 
favor = prefer, or provide 
preferential treatment to 
 
pull themselves up by their 
bootstraps = improve their 
situations by their own effort, 
without assistance 
 
eat, sleep, and breathe = 
constantly be thinking about 
and working with an activity 
 
break it down = explain it and 
make it simple 
 
rationale = reasoning, logical 
sequence of thought 
 
lopsided = unequal; more on 
one side than the other 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Elise: We do our part, though. We donate 
to charity. And I’ve never heard Michael 
make a disparaging remark about poor 
people. Economics aren’t my strong suit, 
but I’m pretty sure he’s not rooting for 
people to starve just so we can get a tax 
break. 
 
Janet: But people are starving. Just look at 
the number of destitute families in our 
soup kitchen every week. In my line of 
work, we have to fight tooth and nail 
against Republican policy. They’re always 
the ones shutting down social programs, 
saying that people shouldn’t be getting 
handouts. Republicans want to keep their 
privileged position while looking down on 
everyone else who isn’t so fortunate.  
 
Elise: Hey – Michael may be a Republican, 
but you can’t make him out to be some 
sort of villain. I’ve pretty much come to 
terms with the fact that he may just have 
different ideas about how to accomplish 
the same goals. He cares about helping 
people, he just doesn’t believe in 
squandering resources on government 
disparaging = insulting and 
disrespectful 
 
not my strong suit = not an area 
in which I’m skilled or 
knowledgeable 
 
rooting for = hoping and wanting 
to happen 
 
starve = suffer and die from lack 
of food 
 
destitute = poor; completely 
lacking resources for survival 
 
soup kitchen = center where 
food is served free to poor 
people 
 
fight tooth and nail = fight 
intensely using all possible 
resources 
 
handouts = things given for free 
 
make him out to be = describe 
him in a certain way 
 
villain = evil person 
 
come to terms with = learned to 
accept and tolerate 
 
squandering = wasting 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
programs with bloated bureaucracies, as 
he puts it. You’re delusional if you think 
Republicans actually want poor people to go 
hungry. 
 
Janet: Sometimes it seems that way.  
 
Elise: And sometimes you sound like a 
broken record. Oh, look at the time. I better 
get going. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
bloated = much bigger than it 
should be 
 
as he puts it = expressing this 
idea in the words that he uses 
 
delusional = holding a 
completely false belief; crazy 
 
you sound like a broken record 
= you keep saying the same 
things repeatedly 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used.

don't see eye to eye 
rooting for 
break it down 
favored 
rub people the wrong way 
come to terms with 
lopsided 
squandering 
delusional 
misleading

ups and downs 
 
1. I can give you some suggestions, but interior design is really 
______________________________. You should ask a pro. 
2. That's a very ______________________________ advertisement - it makes it look like 
you get a free product, but you actually pay full price. 
3. It's very hard to ______________________________ having cancer; a lot of patients 
need counseling. 
4. My teenage daughters were ______________________________ about who would get 
to use the car on Friday night. 
5. Of course we'll be ______________________________ our favorite baseball team to win 
the championship! 
6. Our neighbor is a die-hard atheist who thinks anyone with religious beliefs is 
______________________________. 


 
 
7. She has a bit of an abrasive personality that tends to 
______________________________. 
8. I was always jealous of my little brother because my parents clearly 
______________________________ him. 
9. There's no way I'll be friends with anyone who makes 
______________________________ comments about particular ethnic groups. 
10. We tried to bake a cake, but it came out ______________________________; one part 
was higher than the other. 
11. When I was younger I almost quit piano lessons, but now I'm glad I 
______________________________ it because I really enjoy playing. 
12. I didn't understand today's physics lesson at all. Luckily I found a video online 
that helped ______________________________ for me.

spouse, a friend, colleague, etc.) Describe the difference of opinion and the points
