Lesson 29: Ready for an Adventure? 
 
Steve’s trying to convince his friend Andy to go rock climbing with him. Listen to their 
conversation and answer these eight comprehension questions: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Which sport does Andy prefer? 
a. basketball 
b. football 
c. volleyball 
2. Where does Steve want to go climbing? 
a. at a gym 
b. in another city 
c. on a mountain 
3. What do you have to do before climbing? 
a. buy or rent some equipment 
b. participate in a group class 
c. take a safety training session 
4. What events are often held at the place? 
a. children's parties 
b. climbing competitions 
c. school trips 
5. What sport did Andy's family used to do? 
a. skiing 
b. snowboarding 
c. surfing 
 


 
 
6. What does Steve say is riskier than extreme sports? 
a. driving 
b. flying 
c. smoking 
7. What does Steve love most about climbing? 
a. being outdoors 
b. the mental challenge 
c. the physical exercise 
8. What does Andy suggest doing next weekend? 
a. going to a basketball game 
b. playing tennis 
c. taking his kids to the zoo 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Steve: Any chance you’d be up for some rock 
climbing this weekend? 
 
Andy: Eh, rock climbing isn’t really my thing. 
I’m more of a basketball guy. 
 
Steve: Exactly – you’re tall, you’ve got good 
reach. So you’d probably be a natural at rock-
climbing.  
 
Andy: Okay, I’ll humor you. What have you 
got in mind? 
 
Steve: There’s an indoor gym just twenty 
minutes from here. They’ve got a whole bunch 
of walls – some for beginners, some for 
hardcore climbers. You just have to do a half-
hour training session to learn how to use the 
harness and stuff, and then they turn you 
loose on the walls. 
 
Andy: Hmm. On second thought, I’ve got a 
couple of things to take care of this weekend… 
 
Steve: Don’t chicken out on me! Listen, 
they’re always hosting kids’ birthday parties 
there. If eight-year-old girls can do it, so can 
you. 
 
Andy: Man, just thinking about being fifty feet 
up with nothing but a flimsy harness – it’s 
making my hands sweaty. 
 
you'd be up for = you would 
want to 
 
a natural = someone who has 
natural ability and learns 
quickly 
 
I’ll humor you = I’ll go along 
with what you want in order 
to make you happy 
 
got in mind = thinking about 
 
hardcore = intense 
 
harness = straps that are part 
of the safety equipment 
 
turn you loose = let you go 
freely 
 
on second thought = I’m 
reconsidering this 
 
chicken out = become scared 
and not do something 
 
hosting = having someone or 
something at your place 
 
flimsy = weak, fragile, may 
break easily 
  
Vocabulary 


 
 
Steve: You don’t strike me as the type to 
be afraid of heights. Haven’t you done any 
extreme sports before? 
 
Andy: Uh, what qualifies as an “extreme 
sport”? 
 
Steve: You know, anything that makes 
adrenaline rush through your veins: 
whitewater rafting, jet skiing, 
skydiving, or bungee jumping. That sort 
of thing. 
 
Andy: My family used to ski. Does that 
count? 
 
Steve: Depends. Were you, like, weaving 
in and out of trees, or were you on the 
bunny trail?  
 
Andy: We definitely stayed on the easier 
slopes. I just don’t get why it’s so exciting 
to put your life at risk.  
 
Steve: You know, statistically, your life’s 
more at risk when you’re behind the 
wheel than when you’re skiing or rock 
climbing. Heck, either of us could drop 
dead of a heart attack in the next five 
minutes. Nobody’s invincible. 
 
Andy: OK, I’ll give you that. But I don’t 
see why I should increase my chances by 
flirting with death. 
 
you don’t strike me as = you 
don’t seem like 
 
whitewater rafting = going on an 
inflatable boat in rivers with very 
agitated water 
 
jet skiing = going on the ocean 
with a fast, motorized individual 
boat 
 
skydiving = jumping out of an 
airplane with a parachute 
 
bungee jumping = jumping off a 
bridge or high place with an 
elastic cord tied to your legs 
 
weaving in and out = going 
around the trees to one side of 
each tree and then the other 
 
bunny trail = the least dangerous 
hill, made for children and 
beginner skiers 
 
slopes = hills 
 
I don’t get = I don’t understand 
 
behind the wheel = driving 
 
invincible = unable to be hurt or 
defeated 
 
I’ll give you that = I’ll admit that 
your point is correct 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Steve: It’s hard to explain – I just love the 
nervous anticipation leading up to it – 
will I be able to pull it off? Then when 
you’re finally doing it, you get that surge 
of energy. And afterwards you feel like 
you can take on the world. 
 
Andy: It’s hard to disagree when you get 
all fired up like that. But… I’m a pretty 
big guy, are you sure those ropes can 
hold me? What if they snap? 
 
Steve: Well, just in case, the floor’s 
padded. But trust me, the ropes won’t 
snap – they’ve been tested with over 500 
pounds. Climbing gyms have to meet all 
sorts of safety standards in order to 
operate. 
 
Andy: All right, I guess I’ll give it a shot. 
But next weekend let’s do something 
tamer – like playing tennis. 
 
Steve: Yeah, so you can kick my butt on 
the court to get back at me for making 
you try rock climbing. I haven’t played 
tennis in years, I’m really rusty. 
 
Andy: Hey, I’ve gotta go pick up my 
brother’s kids from day care. Where is 
this rock-climbing gym, anyway? 
 
Steve: I’ll text you the address. 
 
Andy: Cool. Catch ya later.

being killed

something difficult 
 
surge = sudden increase 
 
you can take on the world = you 
can do anything; you can face and 
overcome any challenge 
 
fired up = full of intense emotion 
 
snap = break 
 
padded = covered in soft material 
that will protect you on impact

tamer = less crazy/dangerous

get back at me = get revenge 
 
rusty = performing badly because 
you haven’t practiced in a long time 
 
day care = place where young kids 
are taken care of during the day 
 
catch ya later = see you later

Lesson 30: Losing Your Temper 
 
Listen to this conversation between Jack and his wife Lynn, who lost her temper 
at work. Mark each sentence as “True” or “False.”  
 
Listening Comprehension 
 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
 
1. One of Lynn's colleagues didn't come to work 
2. The restaurant was busy the entire night 
3. The restaurant was featured in a tourist guide 
4. Lynn had to answer a lot of questions  
5. Lynn's boss helped her with the customers 
6. There were children in the group of tourists 
7. The customers were rude to Lynn 
8. Lynn took a break after everyone left 
9. Her boss was angry because Lynn didn't serve everyone fast enough 
10. Lynn was fired from her job 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Jeff: Hey, how was work today? 
 
Lynn: You don’t want to know. I 
don’t have a job anymore. 
 
Jeff: Really? You guys don’t normally 
get tourists. 
 
Lynn: We’ve been getting more lately. 
Someone put us in one of those “off 
the beaten path” guides.  
 
 
Jeff: Ah, so now you get flooded with 
tourists looking for an “authentic” 
place to eat. 
 
Lynn: Yeah. So anyway, here come all 
these tourists, and I’m running 
around like a chicken with its head 
cut off trying to get them seated and 
take their orders. And they’re all 
pestering me with a million questions 
about the menu. I’m just trying to keep 
my cool. 
 
Jeff: Where was your boss? She usually 
pitches in when the place gets busy, 
right? 
 
Lynn: That’s the thing – she was 
nowhere to be found. Finally I get all of 
the drinks served, and then I go in the 
you don’t want to know = the 
answer will not be pleasant to 
hear 
 
shorthanded = lacking the 
necessary number of 
employees 
 
dead = (informal) there were 
no people, no activity 
 
winding down = getting less 
active and preparing to finish 
 
bursts in = comes in quickly 
with lots of energy 
 
off the beaten path = away 
from the main tourist areas 
 
flooded = filled (possibly with 
too much/many) 
 
running around like a chicken 
with its head cut off = moving 
around crazily, without 
direction or organization 
 
pestering me = bothering me 
persistently 
 
keep my cool = stay calm 
 
pitches in = helps 
Vocabulary 


 
 
back to look for a high chair and three more booster seats. 
 
Jeff: Oh no, there were children? 
 
Lynn: Soooo many children. I gathered 
that it was some kind of homeschooling 
group on a field trip. Anyway, I’m back 
there looking around frantically for a 
booster seat, and I hear my boss calling 
my name from the office. I go to the 
office and I’m like, “what?” She starts 
asking me about my tickets from last 
night, and I told her I couldn’t talk about 
it because I was swamped with tables. 
She just frowned and said to come talk 
to her about it as soon as I could. 
 
Jeff: Did she offer to help? 
 
Lynn: Nope. So I just dashed back out 
front and started scribbling down 
orders. It wasn’t that bad, actually. 
Everyone was pretty patient because 
they could see that the place was a 
madhouse and I was the only server. 
 
Jeff: That’s good. I hate it when people 
can’t just chill out and wait.  
 
Lynn: The customers were nice, but the 
cooks were pretty pissed off when they 
got all those orders in the window at 
once.  
 
 
high chair = a raised chair for 
a baby to sit in 
 
booster seats = plastic seats 
placed on top of a regular 
chair so that a small child can 
reach the table 
 
I gathered = I figured out 
from observation 
 
field trip = trip as part of an 
educational experience 
 
frantically = anxiously and 
with a sense of urgency 
 
I’m like = I said (informal) 
 
I was swamped = I had far 
too much work to do 
 
frowned = made an upset 
expression on her face 
 
dashed = ran a short distance 
 
scribbling down = writing 
very fast and sloppily 
 
a madhouse = a crazy, 
chaotic place 
 
chill out = relax 
 
pissed off = angry 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Jeff: I’d be grouchy, too, if I had to make 
30 entrees at the tail end of my shift. 
 
Lynn: They were basically throwing the 
plates at me. But I got everything served, 
and once the checks were paid, the 
whole place just cleared out at once. I 
figured I’d take a breather before 
cleaning up, so I sat down for a sec. And 
that’s when my boss finally appears and 
yells at me because the tables are dirty! 
She said I was slacking off. And THAT 
was the last straw. 
 
Jeff: Uh-oh. I’m afraid to ask, but… what 
did you do? 
 
Lynn: Took off my apron, threw it at her, 
and stormed out of the place. 
 
Jeff: Heh. I thought you were home a bit 
early. So… what now? 
 
Lynn: Right now I’ll just have a drink and 
veg out in front of the TV a bit. And 
tomorrow… I’ll get cracking on some job 
applications.

the tail end = the final part, 
right at the very end 
 
shift = period of work 
 
take a breather = take a 
quick break 
 
sec = second 
 
slacking off = being lazy and 
not putting in effort to do 
the work you’re supposed to 
be doing 
 
the last straw = the final 
thing that made the 
situation impossible to 
tolerate 
 
apron = a covering for your 
clothes to be used while 
cooking or serving food 
 
stormed out = left angrily 
 
veg out = relax in a mindless 
way 
 
get cracking = start

from my grandparents' driveway. 
2. He ____________________ as he read the letter, so I knew it was bad news. 
3. I ____________________ tried to clean up the house a bit when the doorbell 
rang unexpectedly. 
4. The lifeguard ____________________ into the water to rescue the little boy 
who had gone in too deep. 
5. My son is ____________________ because I didn't let him spend the weekend 
at his friend's house. 
6. OK everyone, we have a lot of work to do. Let's ____________________ so we 
can finish early! 
7. Popular authors’ mailboxes often get ____________________ with fan mail 
from people who love their books. 
8. It's rude to just ____________________ into someone's office - you should 
always knock on the door first. 
9. The city center is ____________________ on Sunday; nobody's around and all 
the shops are closed. 
10. We went to Europe at the ____________________ of summer, when the 
weather was starting to get a bit cooler. 
11. The antiques market starts at 9 AM; around 3 PM it's ____________________. 
12. After the argument, his wife ____________________ of the apartment and 
didn't come back for several hours.

Talk about a time you got angry. What made you so upset? What did you do in 
the situation? Have you ever “lost your temper”? (lost control of your 
words/actions in anger). Alternatively, you can talk about a time someone 
else was angry with you. 
 
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the

Lesson 31: Aging 
 
Stephanie is worried about her grandmother, and confides in her friend Jane. Listen to 
their conversation and answer these eight comprehension questions: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
1. Stephanie says her grandmother... 
a. is going blind 
b. should move out of her house 
c. was in a car accident 
2. Jane's family experienced a similar situation with Jane's... 
a. father 
b. grandfather 
c. great-uncle 
3. When Jane's mom pointed out the difficulty, this person... 
a. became angry 
b. didn't take it seriously 
c. was willing to listen 
4. Eventually, Jane's relative... 
a. got injured while at home 
b. couldn't afford the rent for his house 
c. needed health care around the clock 
5. Now, Jane’s relative is… 
a. depressed 
b. happy 
c. no longer able to speak 
 


 
 
6. Stephanie's grandmother has a disease that affects her... 
a. brain 
b. heart 
c. lungs 
7. Jane suggests that Stephanie's grandmother should... 
a. be more physically active 
b. go out for cake and ice cream 
c. visit Jane's relative 
8. Stephanie thinks her grandmother… 
a. only has time on the weekends 
b. will enjoy it 
c. won’t want to go out 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Jane: Hey girlfriend, how are you doing? 
 
Stephanie: I’m fine. Just a little worried about my 
grandmother. 
 
Jane: How come? Is she OK? 
 
Stephanie: Well, her health is starting to 
deteriorate and odds are she’ll have to go live in a 
retirement home.  
 
Jane: Oh no, I’m sorry. Getting old can really be a 
drag. But moving into an assisted-living facility is 
par for the course when you start getting on in 
years. 
 
Stephanie: The thing is, she really prizes her 
independence, so convincing her to move will be 
an uphill battle. 
 
Jane: My mom was in a similar predicament with 
my grandfather – he could barely walk anymore, 
much less go up and down the stairs – but he 
absolutely refused to move out of his third-floor 
apartment.  
 
Stephanie: I suppose people tend to get set in 
their ways when they get older. So what did your 
mom do? 
 
Jane: Every time she pointed out how much 
difficulty he was having in his home, my 
deteriorate = get worse

good chance; it’s 
probable 
 
a drag = (slang) a burden 
 
par for the course = 
something to be 
expected in that 
situation 
 
getting on in years = 
getting older 
 
prizes = loves, values 
highly, appreciates 
 
an uphill battle = a very 
difficult task 
 
predicament = a 
difficult/complicated 
situation 
 
set in their ways = 
continuing with the 
same habits/routine and 
not open to change 
 
pointed out = brought a 
fact to someone’s 
attention 
Vocabulary 


 
 
grandfather would shrug it off and say he could 
handle it. My mom would try to argue, but he just 
wouldn’t budge.  
 
Stephanie: So did he end up staying in his 
apartment? 
  
Jane: No – but it took an accident to make him see 
the light. He slipped when getting out of the 
shower and broke his hip. After that, he 
grudgingly admitted that an assisted-living place 
would be better. 
 
Stephanie: Ah. And was he able to get used to the 
new place? 
 
Jane: That’s the funny part – once he moved in, he 
loved it! Now he tells everyone that moving there 
was the best decision he ever made. 
 
Stephanie: Haha, that’s great! I hope we can 
convince my grandmother to move. She’s in the 
early stages of Alzheimer’s, and her memories are 
starting to go.  
 
Jane: Oh, I’m sorry to hear that.  
 
Stephanie: We’re afraid she might mix up her pills 
or wander out of the house and get lost – so it 
would really be better for her not to live alone. 
 
Jane: That’s understandable… Hey – I have an idea. 
Why don’t you bring your grandmother to visit my 
grandfather? He speaks so highly of the place 
where he lives, I think he could talk anyone into 
moving there.

ignore it as if it weren’t 
important

wouldn’t change his 
belief 
 
see the light = 
understand clearly

side of your body, where 
your leg joins your torso 
 
grudgingly = reluctantly, 
without wanting to 
 
Alzheimer’s = a disease 
that makes you lose 
your memory and 
thinking/reasoning 
abilities 
 
pills = capsules of 
medicine that you 
swallow 
 
wander = go without a 
specific destination 
 
speaks so highly = says 
so many good things 
about 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Stephanie: That’s brilliant! She hardly ever leaves 
the house, so it would be a fun outing for her. And 
if your grandfather can talk her into moving, that 
would be the icing on the cake. 
 
Jane: Let’s plan it for next weekend.

intelligent

outside the house

an extra good thing

Lesson 32: Inventing Something 
 
Two inventors, Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla, discuss the invention of new 
technology. Listen to their conversation and mark the statements “True” or 
“False”: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
True or false? 
1. Edison is annoyed about the explosion Tesla caused. 
2. Some members of Edison's team like Tesla's ideas. 
3. Tesla has some doubts about the viability of his own theory. 
4. Edison's main concern is the cost. 
5. The public has a high demand for energy. 
6. Edison encourages Tesla to work faster. 
7. Edison made ten thousand attempts before succeeding in his invention. 
8. Tesla believes his technology is superior to Edison's. 
9. Edison asks Tesla to make his equipment more efficient. 
10. Tesla refuses to accept the deal. 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Thomas Edison: Ah, Tesla. Could I have a 
word with you? I’ve heard some 
interesting things through the grapevine 
about your work. 
 
Nikola Tesla: Um, if it’s about the little 
explosion in the lab last week, I promise it’ll 
never happen again! -- 
 
Edison: Hm? Oh, no, it has nothing to do 
with that. I’m talking about your theories 
on energy transfer. It seems your ideas are 
resonating with some of our guys.  
 
Tesla: You mean, the team working on your 
generators? 
 
Edison: Now don’t let this go to your 
head, but some of our top engineers think 
your alternating current theories are 
brilliant. They want to see you take the idea 
and run with it. And frankly, I’m a bit 
curious myself.  
 
Could I have a word with 
you? = This is a polite 
way to ask to talk to 
someone 
 
heard through the 
grapevine = heard 
indirectly (by one person 
telling another, who tells 
another, etc.) 
 
has nothing to do with = 
is completely unrelated 
to 
 
resonating with = 
appealing to, sounding 
interesting 
 
generators = machines 
that can generate 
electricity 
 
don’t let this go to your 
head = don’t let this 
praise/accomplishment 
inflate your ego 
 
run with it = continue it 
 
frankly = honestly 
Vocabulary

telling you – alternating current is more than 
brilliant. It’s the way of the future! The only 
true path forward in the development of 
energy.  
 
Edison: Now, don’t get carried away. It is a 
fascinating idea – in theory. But when it comes 
to actually designing these conductors, then we 
have to think about the cost, and about the 
market for this new energy, not to mention the 
dangers. You know the risks better than anyone 
else. Having two currents running at once? 
People might be electrocuted. You’ll never be 
able to win over the public with technology 
that’s potentially lethal.  
 
Tesla: But we don’t have to find a new market 
for alternating current. The demand is already 
there. People are wild about energy and 
they’re just waiting for – no, begging for the 
right tools so that they can get more of it. 
Alternating current would be a revolution in 
power supply! 
 
Edison: And revolutions involve bloodshed. 
No, sir. With a new idea there is nothing so 
don't get carried 
away = don’t let 
enthusiasm make you 
take action too 
quickly or too much

injured or killed by 
electricity 
 
win over = succeed in 
making people accept 
or like something 
 
lethal = could kill you 
 
wild about = 
extremely excited 
about 
 
begging for = asking 
with a lot of emotion 
and urgency 
 
bloodshed = people 
getting injured or 
killed 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
important as careful deliberation and patience. 
A great deal of patience. If every starry-eyed 
revolutionary went ahead with so little regard 
for the consequences… why, then there’d be 
complete anarchy.  
 
Tesla: But I’m not being hasty – I’ve already 
done my calculations hundreds of times.  
 
Edison: Hundreds of times? That’s nothing. Do 
you know how many different substances I 
tried in my light bulb before I stumbled upon 
the right one? Ten thousand! And that is how 
the careful inventor should do his experiments.   
 
Tesla: I disagree. That is the work of a sloppy 
inventor. When I make my calculations, I make 
them precisely. And when I have finished them, 
they are bulletproof. Mark my words – my 
alternating current will make your direct 
current obsolete.  
 
Edison: That is highly doubtful. But let’s put 
your little theory to the test. You’ve insinuated 
that my motors aren’t efficient enough, isn’t 
that right? 
 
starry-eyed = having 
an unrealistic 
optimistic view 
 
anarchy = complete 
lack of any order; 
chaos 
 
hasty = too quick to 
take action, without 
thinking carefully 
 
stumbled upon = 
found by accident  
 
sloppy = not being 
careful or organized 
 
bulletproof = solid; 
unable to be 
damaged 
 
Mark my words = this 
will definitely happen 
in the future 
 
obsolete = when a 
piece of technology is 
outdated and no 
longer used 
 
insinuated = implied; 
said indirectly 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Tesla: They run slower than molasses.  
 
Edison: And I bet you think you could do 
better. All right, I’ll cut you a deal – if you 
redesign my motors so that they don’t cost this 
company a fortune to maintain, there’s fifty 
thousand dollars in it for you—if you can do it 
in six months.  
 
Tesla: I’ll only need three. Let’s shake on it.

= extremely slow 
 
Let’s shake on it = 
let’s shake hands to 
make the agreement 
official 
Vocabulary

Lesson 33: A Looming Deadline 
 
Ben and Anna are a boyfriend and girlfriend who live together. Listen to their 
conversation about tasks and deadlines, and mark the statements below “True” or 
“False.” 
 
Listening Comprehension 
 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
 
1. Ben and Anna have lived together for eight months 
2. Anna has already cleaned the bathroom 
3. The paper is due tomorrow 
4. Anna has no idea what she’s going to write about 
5. Anna has never wanted to change her habits 
6. Anna doesn't like history 
7. Ben offers to write the paper for her 
8. Ben suggests that she use rewards to motivate herself 
9. Anna thinks that system will work for her 
10. If she starts her next paper early, Ben will take her out to eat 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Ben: Are you… folding laundry? You never fold 
laundry. In the eight months we’ve lived 
together, I’ve always seen you just fling your 
clothes onto the bed. 
 
Anna: I have a paper to write. Nothing 
motivates me to do chores like an urgent 
deadline.  
 
Ben: Ah, that explains why the kitchen is 
spotless. 
 
Anna: Just wait until I take on the bathroom. 
 
Ben: You’d rather scrub our toilet than write a 
paper?! 
 
Anna: I’m just dreading it so bad.  
 
Ben: When’s it due? 
 
Anna: Tomorrow. 
 
Ben: Have you started? Tell me you’ve 
started… 
 
Anna: Kind of. I mean, I’ve got an outline, but 
when I try to actually write the darn thing, it’s 
like I get a mental block. So I get antsy and 
feel compelled to do something productive 
instead – like clean the house. 
looming = being present in a 
threatening way 
 
fling = throw casually and 
carelessly 
 
chores = tasks that must be 
done around the house 
 
spotless = perfectly clean 
 
scrub = rub something hard 
in order to clean it 
 
dreading = anticipating with 
great fear, hate, or 
reluctance 
 
so bad = (informal) very 
much 
 
outline = a plan for the main 
points of the paper 
 
a mental block = your 
thoughts stop and can’t 
proceed or develop 
 
antsy = impatient and 
restless, wanting to move or 
do something 
 
compelled = forced by 
powerful feelings 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Ben: Well, I’m not gonna complain about 
your cleaning frenzy, but… your time’s 
running out, and that paper’s not going to 
write itself. 
 
Anna: I know, I know. I told myself I’d stay 
on top of things this semester. I was going 
to get started early on all my assignments 
and not put them off to the last minute. 
 
Ben: So what happened? 
 
Anna: I just couldn’t keep up. My history 
professor kept piling on the homework, and 
I hate history, so I started procrastinating… 
and now the closer the deadline gets, the 
more I panic, and the more I avoid doing it. 
 
Ben: It’s a vicious cycle. But look at it this 
way – let’s say the paper will take you about 
four hours to write. You could either do it in 
a single day, get it over with, and get on 
with your life… or you could spend weeks 
agonizing over it and then still have to put in 
four hours, only now your back is against 
the wall and it’s even harder to concentrate. 
 
Anna: What you’re saying makes so much 
sense… but it’s a little late for that. I wish I’d 
listened to reason and started weeks ago. But 
that is not what happened, and now I’m at 
the end of my rope! 
 
frenzy = period of intense 
activity 
 
stay on top of things = stay 
updated on things and 
complete them on time 
 
put them off = delay, 
procrastinate 
 
keep up = accompany the 
progress 
 
piling on = giving a very large 
amount 
 
a vicious cycle = a situation 
where one bad thing causes 
another, and the second bad 
thing causes even more of the 
first, etc. 
 
get it over with = finish 
something unpleasant quickly 
 
agonizing = suffering mental 
worry or pain about something 
 
your back is against the wall = 
you’re in a difficult situation 
from which it’s impossible to 
escape 
 
I’m at the end of my rope! = 
desperate; don’t have any 
more energy or patience 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Ben: OK, first of all, step away from the laundry. Just 
sit down at your desk, and focus on writing the first 
sentence. Then the first paragraph. Before you know 
it, you’ll have the whole paper written.  
 
Anna: But what about the bathroom? It is filthy, you 
know… 
 
Ben: Right, because we haven’t cleaned it in weeks – 
so that means it can wait another day. Here’s an idea 
– how about from now on you try to bribe yourself 
into starting early on your assignments? 
 
Anna: How would I do that? 
 
Ben: Tell yourself that if you get a certain amount of 
work done by a certain day, then you can indulge in 
something you like. Sushi, maybe. 
 
Anna: I don’t know… I’d probably just miss the 
deadline and have the sushi anyway to reward 
myself for trying. 
 
Ben: Anna! 
 
Anna: What? I know my weaknesses.  
 
Ben: How about this? Next time you have an assignment, let me know and if you get 
started early, I’ll take you out for sushi as a reward. 
 
Anna: OK, but what can I do for you then? 
 
Ben: You can clean the bathroom to your heart’s content. 
 
filthy = extremely dirty 
 
bribe = get something 
you want by offering a 
reward/incentive 
 
indulge in = give in to 
one of your desires 
 
to your heart’s content 
= as much as you want 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
 
agonizing 
dreading 
get it over with 
scrub 
antsy 
filthy 
keep up 
spotless 
at the end of my rope flinging 
looming 
to my heart's content 
compelled 
frenzy 
put off

_________________________. 
2. He takes very good care of his car - not only is it in great condition, but it's 
also _________________________. 
3. It took five hours to _________________________ all the graffiti off the walls. 
4. I've been _________________________ over whether or not to take the job in 
Australia. What should I do? 
5. My dog was _________________________ after playing in the muddy puddles. 
6. Now that I have my own cell phone, I can chat with my friends

7. The kids always get _________________________ during long car trips. Maybe we 
should fly instead. 
8. I was _________________________ the interview, but it actually wasn't so terrible. 
9. They were eating peanuts and just _________________________ the shells onto the 
sidewalk! 
10. When I hear stories of people suffering, I feel _________________________ to help in 
whatever way I can. 
11. You guys are all more experienced runners, so I'm not sure I can 
_________________________ with you. 
12. The malls are crowded in December because of the Christmas shopping 
_________________________.

Describe one of your favorite subjects/teachers at school. Why did you like the class 
so much? What did you learn? Also, talk about one of your least favorite 
subjects/teachers at school. Why didn’t you like the class? 
 
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the MP3 to 
homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback!

Lesson 34: The Accident 
 
George tells Mrs. Douglas some bad news about the delivery of her piano. Listen 
to their conversation and answer the comprehension questions below: 
Listening Comprehension 
 
1. The piano is supposed to be delivered at... 
a. nine 
b. ten 
c. twelve 
2. George is late because of... 
a. a traffic accident 
b. an accident with the piano 
c. a wrong address 
3. The piano is... 
a. broken 
b. lost 
c. not the right model 
4. Who was responsible for the first incident with the piano? 
a. George 
b. one of the workers 
c. the manufacturer of the piano 
5. Mrs. Douglas needs the piano next week because... 
a. the academy needs to start classes 
b. there will be a competition 
c. there will be a Christmas performance 
6. What happened to the piano at the repair shop? 
a. it fell down the stairs 
b. it was stolen 
c. the incompetent repairman broke it 
7. What is George's solution? 
a. borrowing a piano from another academy 
b. ordering a replacement piano 
c. paying for the piano to be fixed 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
George Willard: Hello? Is this Mrs. Douglas at 
the Yorktown Music Academy?  
 
Mrs. Douglas: Yes, it is. May I ask who’s 
calling? 
 
George: This is George Willard, from 
Willard’s Piano Movers. 
 
Mrs. Douglas: Ah, hello, George! We’re 
expecting you at ten. Everyone’s very excited 
to see the new instrument. There’s even a 
journalist here from the local paper who came 
to take pictures! 
 
George: Mrs. Douglas, I’m afraid we won’t be 
there at ten. 
 
Mrs. Douglas: Oh, it’s perfectly 
understandable if you’re held up by traffic. 
 
George: It’s not that… it’s… well, there’s been 
an accident. 
 
Mrs. Douglas: An accident, Mr. Willard? 
 
George: Actually, more like a catastrophe.  
 
Mrs. Douglas: Oh my goodness! Mr. Willard, 
please tell me about the piano. Is it—is it lost?  
 
George: No ma’am, not lost.  
 
May I ask who’s 
calling? = This is a 
polite phrase to ask 
about the identity of 
the person who 
initiated the phone call 
 
I’m afraid = We can use 
“I’m afraid” to 
introduce bad news. It 
doesn’t mean you’re 
literally scared 
 
held up = delayed 
 
catastrophe = a HUGE 
disaster 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Mrs. Douglas: Well then, what 
happened? Where is the piano? 
 
George: It’s here at the warehouse, it’s 
just… in no condition to be played. 
 
Mrs. Douglas: Please, please don’t tell 
me— 
 
George: I’m afraid so. You see, our lift 
was on the fritz so we had to load the 
piano into the truck manually. And one 
of our guys, well, he got butterfingers. 
 
Mrs. Douglas: Butterfingers? 
 
George: This particular worker is 
normally very conscientious. But this 
time I think he just got a little nervous. I 
mean—it’s not every day you handle a 
$250,000 piano.   
 
Mrs. Douglas: Mr. Willard, please cut to 
the chase. 
 
George: As I was saying, our boy was a 
little high-strung and I guess he either 
didn’t strap the harness on correctly, or 
maybe his fingers just didn’t have a good 
grip. Next thing we knew the piano 
crashed down to the ground.  
 
Mrs. Douglas: Oh, this is terrible! What I 
am going to tell the board of directors? 
We have pianists who’ve flown in from all 
warehouse = a building 
where items are stored 
 
on the fritz = not working 
 
manually = by hand, 
without the help of 
machines or automatic 
processes 
 
butterfingers = when 
something slips out of your 
hands, you can say you have 
“butterfingers” 
 
conscientious = careful, 
paying attention to details 
 
it’s not every day = it’s 
rather rare 
 
cut to the chase = get 
directly to the main point 
 
high-strung = nervous and 
tense 
 
harness = strips of material 
that hold something and 
prevent it from falling 
 
grip = the strength of your 
hold on something 
 
board of directors = group 
of people who guide a 
company or organization 
Vocabulary 


 
 
over the world for the competition next week! 
 
George: Well ma’am, forgive me if I’m out 
of line, but maybe you can take some 
comfort in the fact that the instrument you 
purchased was a real work of art. One-of-a-
kind craftsmanship, and durable as the 
Appalachian Mountains.  
 
Mrs. Douglas: Mr. Willard, how can you 
have the gall to suggest that our players 
perform on an instrument that’s been 
dropped on the ground? 
 
George: Actually, that’s precisely what I’d 
suggest if that’d been the end of it. Truth be 
told, there were only a couple of scrapes on 
the instrument after the first fall. 
 
Mrs. Douglas: The first fall?   
 
George: You see, we took a slight detour in 
order to touch up the varnish on the piano, 
and at the repair shop, there were some 
steps we had to navigate. The piano started 
to tip over and before we could balance it, 
it tumbled down the stairs.  
 
Mrs. Douglas: Mr. Willard, that is enough! I 
am simply astounded at your 
incompetence. How could you let a 
priceless work of art fall off a truck and 
down a stairwell?! I just want to know how 
and when you are going to fix it!  
 
out of line = 
inappropriate 
 
durable = strong and 
long-lasting 
 
have the gall = have the 
courage/arrogance (also 
“have the nerve”) 
 
Truth be told = Honestly 
 
scrapes = damage caused 
by rubbing off the outer 
surface of the material 
 
detour = different route 
from the planned path 
 
touch up = make small 
repairs/improvements to 
 
tip over = incline, lose 
balance and start to fall 
 
astounded = extremely 
surprised and shocked 
 
incompetence = lack of 
knowledge and common 
sense 
 
priceless = extremely 
valuable 
 
stairwell = set of stairs 
Vocabulary 


 
 
George: Your outrage is certainly justified, 
ma’am. But I’ve already taken the liberty 
of ordering you a new piano of the same 
model. The manufacturer understands the 
emergency and is expediting the shipment, 
so we’ll bring it to you the moment it’s 
ready.  
 
Mrs. Douglas: Well that’s some good news! 
When can we expect it?   
 
George: Three to four months, ma’am.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
outrage = strong anger 
 
taken the liberty of = 
done without asking 
permission first 
 
expediting = processing 
faster than normal 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
 
catastrophe 
grip 
high-strung 
on the fritz 
scrape 
conscientious 
had the gall incompetent out of line 
taken the liberty 
durable 
held up 
manually 
outraged 
tip over 
 
 
1. Does she cut your hair _______________________, or does she use an electric 
shaver? 
2. Hi, nice to see you! I've _______________________ of ordering you a drink - I 
hope you like margaritas. 
3. If you tend to be _______________________, you should probably avoid jobs 
which are dangerous and stressful. 
4. There's a _______________________on the side of my car from where a kid 
ran into it with a bicycle. 
5. It's really hot in the office because our air conditioner's 
_______________________. 
6. The construction project is currently _______________________ because 
we're waiting for permits from the city. 
7. The oil spill was an environmental _______________________ - it killed a lot 
of wildlife and polluted the beaches. 
8. Be careful! If you bump into the table, the wedding cake could 
_______________________. 
9. This backpack is extremely _______________________ - I've taken it on years 
of hiking trips and it's still in great condition. 
10. When the murderer got a very light sentence, the victim's family was 
_______________________. 
11. You were definitely speeding - so you were _______________________ when 
you started arguing with the police officer. 
12. I'm looking for an accountant who's _______________________, because we 
need to record every single detail of the finances. 
 


 
 
Speaking Task 
Imagine you are Mrs. Douglas – what would you do in this situation?  
• Would you cancel the piano competition, or would you try to get 
another piano quickly? (How?)  
• Would you be angry with George, or would you appreciate his efforts to 
help?  
• Would you use George’s company again, or not?  
• How would you explain this whole situation to the board of directors? 
 
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the 
MP3 to homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback!

2. b 
3. a

5. b 
6. a 
7. b

3. high-strung

Lesson 35: A Bit of Gossip 
 
Caryn and Lucy are two high school students. Listen to them gossip about another girl 
they know, Jennifer, and mark the statements below “True” or “False.” 
 
Listening Comprehension 
 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
 
1. Jennifer was punished for fighting with Dan in the hallway 
2. Caryn and Lucy have seen Jennifer's new boyfriend before 
3. Jennifer's relationships tend to last a long time 
4. Caryn and Lucy frequently get asked out on dates 
5. Jennifer's boyfriends don't attend the same high school 
6. Jennifer was very upset after her last relationship ended 
7. Jennifer doesn't want Caryn and Lucy to date her ex-boyfriends 
8. Jennifer is on her way to lunch with her new boyfriend 
9. Caryn and Lucy don’t want to be friends with Jennifer anymore 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Lucy: So did you hear the latest about Jennifer? 
 
Caryn: About how she got detention for 
talking back to the choir teacher?  
 
Lucy: No, no, that’s old news. This is something 
even juicier. 
 
Caryn: Did she have another spat with Dan? 
 
Lucy: Close, but no cigar. 
 
Caryn: Well come on, don’t keep me in 
suspense!  
 
Lucy: OK, OK. Get a load of this – Jennifer’s 
still with Dan, but I heard from Vanessa that 
she’s also seeing that guy from Rockford High. 
You remember – the one from the football 
team. 
 
Caryn: You mean Jason? The one we were 
drooling over at the party on Saturday night? 
Yeah, of course I remember him! 
 
Lucy: That's the one. Apparently he has quite 
the reputation as a ladies’ man – and he’s got 
his own car. Vanessa says that he and Jennifer 
were making out in the park yesterday. 
 
Caryn: It’s so unfair! Jennifer gets all the hot 
guys. What’s her secret? 
 
detention = a punishment in 
which a student must stay 
extra time after school 
 
talking back = replying in a 
disrespectful way 
 
juicier = more 
interesting/scandalous 
 
spat = a quick 
fight/argument 
 
Close, but no cigar = You’re 
almost correct, but not 
completely correct 
 
Get a load of this = look at / 
listen to this especially 
interesting thing 
 
seeing = dating, romantically 
involved with 
 
drooling over = deeply 
desiring 
 
a ladies’ man = a man who is 
popular with women 
 
making out = kissing 
passionately 
 
hot = sexy, attractive 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Lucy: Well, I have a hunch that her skimpy 
clothes probably have a lot to do with it. But 
it’s not like her relationships last… I mean, 
Dan is what, her third boyfriend so far this 
year? 
 
Caryn: That’s because no guy wants to stay 
with her once they discover how shallow 
she is. Meanwhile, nobody ever asks me out. 
 
Lucy: I’m in the same boat. Seems like it 
doesn’t matter how great of a person you 
are, the prettier girls always steal the show. 
 
Caryn: So, Jennifer and Jason… could you 
imagine what would happen if Dan caught 
wind of this? 
 
Lucy: Jennifer’s probably doing everything 
in her power to make sure the two don’t 
cross paths. They do go to different schools, 
after all. 
 
Caryn: Yeah, but she’s not the sharpest 
tool in the shed. She’s bound to slip up 
some time, and then both guys will dump 
her. 
 
Lucy: Which is what she deserves. But then 
you and I will have to deal with the fallout. 
After her last breakup she was a basket 
case for a whole month. 
 
Caryn: Not to mention the fact that she’d 
give us the cold shoulder if we ever dared 
to date one of her exes. 
a hunch = a strong feeling or 
suspicion 
 
skimpy clothes = clothes that 
don’t cover much of the body 
 
shallow = not having deep or 
complex knowledge or 
personality 
 
in the same boat = in the same 
situation 
 
steal the show = get all the 
attention 
 
caught wind of = heard about 
or found out about 
 
cross paths = accidentally meet 
someone 
 
not the sharpest tool in the 
shed = stupid, not intelligent 
 
slip up = make a mistake 
 
dump her = end the romantic 
relationship with her 
 
fallout = the negative results of 
a disaster 
 
a basket case = a person who is 
too upset/nervous to function 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Lucy: Seriously! And I had a crush on Dan all last 
year, but he only had eyes for Jennifer. Now I’ll 
never have a shot. 
 
Jennifer: Hey girls! What’s up? 
 
Lucy: (startled) Oh hi Jennifer, what a coincidence! 
We were just saying how great you looked at the 
party last weekend. 
 
Caryn: Yeah and what a catch that guy from 
Rockford is. Are you two an item now? 
 
Jennifer: Sort of. It’s complicated. Actually, I’m off 
to watch his football practice right now. I’ll see you 
two at lunch tomorrow. 
 
Lucy: OK, have fun!  
 
Caryn: Whew, that was close. Do you think she 
overheard us talking about her?  
 
Lucy: I don't think so – otherwise she would’ve 
said something to our faces. But we should 
probably be a little more careful next time. 
 
Caryn: I know, I would be mortified if she found 
out what we really think. If it weren't for Jennifer 
we would never be part of the popular crowd.  
 
Lucy: Our social lives would be over in a 
heartbeat. 
 
 
 
give us the cold shoulder 
= ignore, not be friendly 
to 
 
exes = former romantic 
partners 
 
had a crush on = was 
romantically attracted to 
 
only had eyes for = was 
only interested in 
 
have a shot = have a 
chance 
 
a catch = (informal) a 
great person to have a 
romantic relationship 
with 
 
an item = a couple that is 
romantically involved 
 
to our faces = directly to 
us 
 
mortified = extremely 
embarrassed 
 
in a heartbeat = instantly 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
 
catch wind of 
giving me the cold shoulder 
made out with 
cross paths 
hare a crush 
mortified 
drooling over 
have a shot 
slipped up 
dumped 
hunch 
spats 
in a heartbeat 
in the same boat 
stole the show 
 
 
1. All the actors were good, but Tom absolutely ________________________ with his 
performance. 
2. Christine ________________________ her last boyfriend because he didn't spend 
enough time with her. 
3. I have a ________________________ that he's not telling me the whole story, but I 
can't prove it. 
4. Our flight was canceled, too, so we're ________________________. 
5. I was ________________________ when I clogged the toilet at my new boyfriend's 
house. 
6. My brother and I have a pretty good relationship. We sometimes have 
________________________, but we don't stay mad at each other for long. 
7. On my first day on the job, I ________________________ and called my boss by the 
wrong name! 
8. Our neighbors have a totally different schedule, so we don't 
________________________ very often. 
9. We can't let the media ________________________ this, otherwise it'll be a disaster 
for the company. 
10. When my husband bought a brand-new motorcycle, all his friends were 
________________________ it. 
11. I think I ________________________ at getting that job - I have all the qualifications 
they're looking for. 
12. My cousin's been ________________________  ever since I criticized her taste in 
music. 


 
 
Speaking Task 
 
Talk about your experience in high school. Were you popular? Did you care about 
what other people thought about you? What activities were you involved in? Did you 
have any significant friendships or relationships? 
 
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the MP3 to 
homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback! 
 
 
 
Answers 
 
Comprehension Questions 
1. False 
2. True 
3. False 
4. False 
5. True 
6. True 
7. True 
8. False 
9. False 
Vocabulary Quiz

2. dumped 
3. hunch 
4. in the same boat 
5. mortified 
6. spats 
7. slipped up 
8. cross paths 
9. catch wind of

12. giving me the cold shoulder

Lesson 36: Immigration Debate 
Paul and Jennifer are brother and sister. They have different views about 
immigration. Listen to their conversation as you answer these questions: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
1. What is Paul’s view on immigration? 
a. He is in favor of it 
b. He is against it 
c. He is neutral 
 
2. Jennifer insinuates that Paul’s beliefs are affected by his… 
a. parents 
b. social status 
c. romantic relationship 
 
3. Paul's friend... 
a. hasn't been back to his country in thirty years 
b. tried unsuccessfully to get into the U.S. for thirty years 
c. was deported after thirty years in the U.S. 
 
4. Which of these is NOT mentioned as a negative point to 
immigration? 
a. Increased crime 
b. Overcrowding in cities 
c. Fewer jobs for citizens 
 
5. What is the solution proposed for the tax issue? 
a. Reduce the number of public services 
b. Increase taxes on native-born citizens 
c. Make illegal immigrants legal 


 
 
 
Conversation Text 
Paul: Mom and Dad can be so close-minded 
when it comes to certain issues. It drives me 
nuts. 
 
Jennifer: For instance…? 
 
Paul: Well, immigration is the obvious one. 
 
Jennifer: I guess that’s a touchy subject for you 
since your girlfriend’s from Guatemala.  
 
Paul: True, but my position on the topic would be 
the same either way. Hear me out – the United 
States was built by immigrants. It seems so 
hypocritical to now all of a sudden decide we can 
pick and choose who we’ll accept and who we’ll 
shut out.  
 
Jennifer: I think it’s probably more complicated 
than that. 
 
Paul: Seems pretty clear-cut to me. I mean – it’s 
not easy to immigrate to a new country with a 
strange language and leave your family behind. 
People don’t do it because they want to. They do it 
because they have to. Case in point – I know a guy 
who hasn’t been able to return to his homeland in 
thirty years. He hasn’t seen his parents in all that 
time, because if he ever goes home, he’s not sure 
he can come back to the U.S. And since he just 
can’t make a living at home, he stays here.  
 
Jennifer: Wow. If he was willing to make such 
close-minded = not 
tolerant of other 
beliefs; not willing to 
consider other views 
 
it drives me nuts = it 
really annoys me 
 
for instance = for 
example 
 
a touchy subject = a 
sensitive / delicate 
topic 
 
Hear me out = Listen 
to everything I have to 
say on this point 
 
hypocritical = having a 
contradiction in 
beliefs and actions 
 
shut out = exclude, 
not permit to enter 
 
clear-cut = clear and 
obvious 
 
Case in point = the 
following example 
demonstrates my 
point perfectly 
 
make a living = earn 
enough money to 
survive 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
sacrifices, it must be near impossible to make a 
decent living in his country.  
 
Paul: Exactly. We shouldn’t be such a heartless 
nation that we refuse to let people in, and force them 
to hide by living illegally. We should welcome 
immigrants with open arms. There’s more than 
enough room for everyone. 
 
Jennifer: Well… from what I’ve heard, there have 
been some complications with the surge of 
immigration in recent years. If unchecked, it would 
make the country go downhill pretty fast. 
 
Paul: Hmm… that’s probably scaremongering by 
conservatives in order to support their points… but 
what have you heard? 
 
Jennifer: Basically, a large influx of immigrants can 
lead to a rise in poverty, an increase in crime and 
more crowding in the cities. Not to mention the 
strain on the public systems, since illegal 
immigrants don’t pay taxes. Doesn’t it make sense to 
you that at some point we just can’t accommodate 
everybody? 
 
Paul: Yeah, but I think that those disaster scenarios 
are so far off we shouldn’t take them seriously – at 
least, not right now. The obvious solution is to make 
it easier to immigrate legally. People always 
complain that immigrants don’t pay taxes, right? 
There’s a simple fix to that – make them legal! 
Immigrants would be happy to pay taxes. It’d be a 
small price to pay in order to live without fear of 
getting deported, and the country would have 
increased revenue. Seems like a win-win to me. 
heartless = cruel, 
without compassion 
 
welcome with open 
arms = welcome 
enthusiastically 
 
more than enough = 
lots of extra, much 
more than the 
minimum amount 
 
surge = big increase 
 
unchecked = not 
stopped or reduced 
 
go downhill = get 
worse 
 
scaremongering = 
spreading very 
frightening rumors 
 
not to mention = in 
addition; plus 
 
strain = dangerous 
increased pressure 
 
a small price to pay = 
a relatively small 
sacrifice to make, 
when compared with 
the great benefits 
received 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
 
Jennifer: Sounds like you’ve solved all the 
country’s problems. Maybe you should run for 
president. 
 
Paul: Hey, you never know! 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
win-win = a situation 
that’s good for both 
sides 
 
run for president = try 
to be elected 
president 
 
you never know! = it 
could be a possibility; 
it’s not impossible 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
Complete the sentences with these words: 
 
clear-cut 
heartless 
strain 
close-minded 
make a living 
surge 
driving me nuts 
more than enough 
touchy subject 
going downhill 
 
 
1. Be careful with that box - it's pretty heavy, and you don't want to 
________________________ your back. 
2. He got a ________________________ of fan mail after one of his songs was 
featured in a popular TV show. 
3. It's a complex problem, so there's no ________________________ solution. 
4. My boss never listens to suggestions. He's pretty ________________________. 
5. Please stop tapping your foot - it's ________________________! 
6. Religion can be a ________________________, so it's probably better not to 
discuss it on a first date. 
7. She dropped out of business school and is now trying to 
________________________  from her art. 
8. The parents were arrested for torturing their child. How could they be 
so ________________________?! 
9. Their relationship is ________________________ - I think they're headed for a 
breakup. 
10. We don't need to buy any more food for the party; we already have 
________________________. 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
Speaking Task 
Imagine that Paul and Jennifer then turned to you and asked, “So, what do you 
think about all this?” Explain your point of view on immigration, giving the 
reasons for your opinions.  
 
Record your 1-3 minute answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish - or, 
if you prefer, you can e-mail me the MP3 to homework@espressoenglish.net 
for feedback on your spoken English. 
 
 
 
Answers 
 
Comprehension Questions 
1. a 
2. c 
3. a 
4. c 
5. c 
 
Vocabulary Quiz

2. surge 
3. clear-cut 
4. close-minded 
5. driving me nuts 
6. touchy subject 
7. make a living 
8. heartless 
9. going downhill 
10. more than enough

Lesson 37: Different Tastes 
 
Two friends, Grace and Erica, discuss their preferences. Listen to their conversation 
and mark the statements below “True” or “False”: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
True or false according to the conversation? 
1. Grace had a very busy weekend 
2. Erica went to the Lucky Lark with her boyfriend 
3. There is plenty of space inside the café  
4. Erica was not pleased with the service 
5. Erica was given the wrong dish twice 
6. Grace thinks the Dragon's Den is awful 
7. Erica especially likes the pizza there 
8. The Dragon's Den is always full during the day 
9. Erica has never tried Mexican food 
10. Erica agrees to have lunch with Grace 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Erica: Hey Grace. How was your weekend? 
 
Grace: Mmm, pretty uneventful. We spent most 
of it tinkering with our new sound system, trying 
to get it all set up. Oh! We did stop by that new 
café near the library – it’s called the Lucky Lark. 
Have you heard of it? 
 
Erica: Yeah, my boyfriend dragged me there last 
week. Not my cup of tea. 
 
Grace: What? Why? The seating area’s a little 
cramped, but we thought it was charming. I 
loved all the old movie posters on the walls. And 
the food was terrific. 
 
Erica: I don’t know, it just seems like it’s trying 
too hard to be trendy. And when we went, our 
server seemed absent-minded – she forgot our 
drinks twice.  
 
Grace: Well, the place is new, and I’m sure they’re 
still trying to work out the kinks in the system.  
 
uneventful = not busy, 
not much happened 
 
tinkering = making small 
attempts to fix or change 
a machine or system 
 
stop by = visit quickly 
 
dragged me = brought me 
when I didn’t want to go 
 
not my cup of tea = I 
didn’t like it 
 
cramped = there is little 
space 
 
charming = nice, 
enjoyable, pleasant 
 
trendy = fashionable, cool 
 
absent-minded = 
forgetful, distracted 
 
work out the kinks = 
resolve the small 
problems or mistakes 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Erica: While they’re at it, they might want to 
pay a little more attention to their food. It was 
hit and miss – the pasta my boyfriend 
ordered was all right, but I got a sandwich and 
the bread was stale.  
 
Grace: So why didn’t you send it back? 
 
Erica: Eh, we were already running late, so I 
just decided to grin and bear it. I just don’t 
get how they can charge so much for crummy 
service and food that’s only so-so.  
 
Grace: I thought it was worth every penny. 
They have a really creative cocktail menu, 
and we thought all the food was really 
inventive and fresh. We got this amazing 
cucumber and peach salad, steamed brussels 
sprouts with apple sauce, and stuffed 
butternut squash.  
 
Erica: To each their own. I’d rather go to the 
Dragon’s Den any day. 
 
Grace: Ugh, that hole in the wall? It’s so dark 
and grungy. 
 
While they’re at it = while 
they are doing that 
 
hit and miss = sometimes 
good, sometimes bad; not 
consistently good 
 
stale = if bread is stale, it 
means it is old and hard, not 
very fresh 
 
grin and bear it = stay in a 
good mood while enduring a 
bad situation  
 
crummy = bad 
 
so-so = mediocre, not very 
good 
 
worth every penny = valuable 
enough to justify the price 
 
cocktail = mixed drinks (ex. 
alcohol and fruit juice) 
 
steamed = cooked with water 
vapor 
 
to each their own = every 
person has their own 
preferences 
 
hole in the wall = a small 
place 
 
grungy = dirty, smelly 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Erica: But they have huge cheeseburgers, and the 
best chicken wings in the state. And the service is 
super-fast. 
 
Grace: Probably because you’re the only one in 
there. It’s a mystery to me how that place even 
keeps the lights on. 
 
Erica: They pull a big late-night crowd. Things start 
picking up around midnight. 
 
Grace: Ah, that makes sense. People who are 
wasted aren’t as picky about their food. And they 
don’t care if the kitchen is infested with 
cockroaches. 
 
Erica: All I know is that you can eat your fill for less 
than ten bucks, and the people who hang out there 
aren’t pretentious.  
 
Grace: You don’t have to be pretentious to enjoy 
healthy food. Do they even serve salad at the 
Dragon’s Den? 
 
Erica: They put lettuce and tomato on the burgers. 
 
Grace: That doesn’t count. Is that all you’re willing 
to eat? Burgers? 
keeps the lights on = 
stays in business (has 
enough money to pay 
the bills, such as the 
electric bill) 
 
things start picking up 
= the amount of activity 
starts increasing 
 
wasted = (slang) drunk 
 
picky = selective 
 
infested = full of insects 
 
eat your fill = eat as 
much as you need to 
satisfy your hunger 
 
pretentious = claiming 
or behaving as if you 
are superior to others 
 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Erica: Nope. I like Mexican food, too. 
 
Grace: OK. I know a Mexican place downtown, 
wanna go there for lunch? 
 
Erica: Depends. Do they have normal Mexican food? 
None of this fusion cuisine nonsense? 
 
Grace: No fusion, but it’s mostly a vegan Mexican 
place. 
 
Erica: Oh. Then I’ll pass. I’m not eating a taco full of 
radishes. I’ll be hungry again in an hour. 
 
Grace: It’s not totally vegan. They have fish tacos. 
Come on… my treat. 
 
Erica: Well… all right. I’ll give this place a try. Hope 
they have good guacamole. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
downtown = in the city 
center 
 
fusion = 
combining/mixing two 
things 
 
nonsense = something 
that is silly and not to 
be taken seriously 
 
vegan = not 
using/eating any animal 
products at all 
 
I’ll pass = I won’t 
accept this 
invitation/opportunity 
 
my treat = I’ll pay for 
you 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
absent-minded 
hit and miss 
picky 
wasted 
dragging me 
nonsense 
so-so 
working out the kinks 
grin and bear it 
pass 
stop by 
worth every penny 
grungy 
picking up 
tinkering 
 
 
1. I really hate being around my cousin, but at my sister's wedding I just had to 
__________________________. 
2. We can't use a machine whose safety record is __________________________. Our 
equipment has to be completely reliable. 
3. My parents are going on vacation; they might __________________________ around 
10 to say goodbye. 
4. Leather jackets may be pricey, but they're __________________________ because 
they last a long time. 
5. My dad is an engineer and he's always enjoyed __________________________ with 
his car. 
6. I thought the movie was __________________________. It was somewhat 
entertaining, but I probably wouldn't watch it again. 
7. Our ice cream shop doesn't get many customers in the winter, but when the 
weather gets warm then things start __________________________. 
8. That's the third time this week you've locked your keys in the car! How can 
you be so __________________________? 
9. I don't have much free time, so I'm very __________________________ about what I 
choose to commit to.

Lesson 38: Health Problems 
 
Rick asks his friend Danny for help in his exercise routine. Listen to their conversation 
and choose the best answer for each comprehension question: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
 
1. This is Rick's first workout after... 
a. being diagnosed with a disease 
b. having surgery 
c. recovering from a concussion 
2. Danny suggests beginning the workout with... 
a. jogging 
b. stretching 
c. weightlifting 
3. Rick wants to change his... 
a. appearance 
b. diet 
c. lifestyle 
4. Danny warns him that he could get... 
a. dehydrated 
b. frustrated 
c. injured 
5. What does Rick want to do next month? 
a. a boxing competition 
b. a marathon 
c. join the military 
 


 
 
6. Rick has been taking his pills... 
a. regularly 
b. inconsistently 
c. too frequently 
7. He hasn't told his doctor that the medication gives him... 
a. back pain 
b. headaches 
c. stomach problems 
8. Danny doesn't want to... 
a. continue with the workout 
b. offend Rick 
c. talk about health problems constantly 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Danny: Hey, Rick! Glad you could make it! 
 
Rick: Yeah man, I’m pumped! So what are we 
going to start out with? Bench pressing?  
 
Danny: Um, seeing as this is your first workout 
after your operation… we should probably start 
with something more low-key. 
 
Rick: What do you mean… like push-ups? Sit-
ups? 
 
Danny: Dude – baby steps. Let’s warm up with a 
few laps around the track. You ready? 
 
Rick: Oh, come on! Jogging around the track? I 
could have done that at home. I was hoping we 
could get into something a little more challenging! 
 
Danny: It’s important to take it slow, Rick. You 
don’t want to overwork your heart. 
 
Rick: But I can’t let my heart condition define me! 
I’m totally ready to change my lifestyle. No more 
being a couch potato! 
make it = come, attend 
an event 
 
pumped = very excited 
(informal) 
 
bench pressing = a 
weightlifting exercise 
where you lay on your 
back and push a weight 
up and away from your 
chest 
 
low-key = relaxed, less 
intense 
 
push-ups/sit-ups = 
different types of 
exercises for your arms 
and your abdomen, 
respectively 
 
baby steps = make small 
bits of progress towards a 
goal 
 
laps = a “lap” is one 
complete journey around 
a circuit, like a racetrack 
 
couch potato = a lazy 
person who doesn’t 
exercise or move much 
Vocabulary 


 
 
 
Danny: OK, I applaud your enthusiasm – but 
that’s all the more reason to ease into your 
new routine. If you bite off more than you 
can chew, you could get hurt – and an injury 
would put you out of commission for weeks 
or even months. Don’t worry – we’ll build up 
to the tougher stuff. 
 
Rick: I hope so. I signed up for a marathon 
next month. Hope you can whip me into 
shape in time! 
 
Danny: Wait a minute! A marathon? Are you 
sure you’re ready for that? 
 
Rick: Well, not right now, but I should be by 
next month, right? 
 
Danny: Rick, I wouldn’t count on that. In fact, I 
don’t want to rain on your parade, but… it’s 
possible that with your heart issues, you may 
never be able to run a marathon. 
 
Rick: I don’t get it. Why are you trying to 
undermine my progress? 
 
applaud = express approval 
and praise 
 
all the more reason = an even 
better/stronger reason 
 
ease into = enter a situation 
slowly and carefully 
 
bite off more than you can 
chew = take on too much so 
that you can’t handle it 
 
out of commission = not able 
to function 
 
build up to = develop into 
something greater 
 
marathon = an athletic event 
where you run 26.2 miles 
 
whip me into shape = train 
me hard and fast so that my 
physical condition improves 
 
rain on your parade = ruin 
your plans/happiness 
 
undermine = make 
something weaker by 
damaging its base 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Danny: I’m just trying to keep things realistic. You do 
have a heart condition, which means you need to do 
light workouts, and take your medication. You have 
been taking your pills, right? 
 
Rick: Sure… you know, on and off. 
 
Danny: What’s that supposed to mean?! 
 
Rick: Well, some days I feel a little better than others, 
so I don’t take my meds. I save ‘em up for the times 
when I’m feeling under the weather. 
 
Danny: What?! Those pills are supposed to regulate 
your blood pressure. You don’t just take them 
whenever you feel like it! I think you should talk to 
your doctor… 
 
Rick: Aw, doctors don’t know everything! They always 
just wanna prescribe more pills so they get the patient 
off their back. Plus, the medication sometimes makes 
me queasy. 
 
Danny: Have you told your doctor about that? 
 
Rick: I will eventually. When I get around to it. 
 
on and off = 
sometimes yes, 
sometimes no (not 
consistently) 
 
meds = medication 
 
under the weather = 
not feeling well 
physically 
 
regulate = keep 
stable and 
consistent, without 
letting it get too high 
or too low 
 
off their back = stop 
bothering them 
 
queasy = feeling sick 
in your stomach, like 
you might vomit 
 
get around to = 
manage to do 
sometime despite a 
busy schedule 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Danny: OK, Rick, I’ll just say it point-blank – you need 
to take better care of yourself.  
 
Rick: Hey, I’m here at the gym, aren’t I? I’m trying to 
deal with my health problems. What more do you 
want? 
 
Danny: I’m sorry, but I’m gonna have to bow out. You 
need to get your doctor’s okay before we go ahead 
with these exercise sessions.  
 
Rick: But that could be a real hassle!  
 
Danny: Maybe, but it’s for your own good.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
say it point-blank = 
say it directly 
 
bow out = remove 
myself from the 
situation, not 
participate 
 
get your doctor’s 
okay = get your 
doctor’s approval 
 
hassle = something 
that is difficult and 
complicated 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Vocabulary Quiz 
 
Complete each sentence with a word from the box. Three words are not used. 
 
baby steps 
hassle 
off my back 
pumped 
build up to 
laps 
on and off 
queasy 
ease into 
low-key 
out of commission 
under the weather 
get around to 
make it 
point-blank 
 
 
1. There will be a few smaller events during the week to ________________________ 
the big show on Saturday. 
2. My cousin is an alcoholic, but he's taking ________________________ towards 
getting sober. It's slow, but he's making progress. 
3. I'd rather not go sailing - I always get ________________________ when I'm on a 
boat. 
4. It's a ________________________ to get a new passport if you lose yours while 
traveling. 
5. My car needs a few new parts for the engine, so it'll be ________________________ 
for the next few days. 
6. Everyone is ________________________ for the Brazil-Argentina soccer game 
tonight! 
7. My sister's been dating ________________________ for the past few years, but she 
hasn't had any serious relationships. 
8. I don't really like clubbing. I prefer a ________________________ get-together like 
hanging out at a friend's house. 
9. Sorry, but I won't be able to ________________________ to the party. Wish Tim a 
happy birthday for me! 
10. The company's giving me a lot of training, so I'll be able to 
________________________ my new role as chief engineer. 
11. My wife's been asking me constantly to clean the garage - I wish she'd get 
________________________! 
12. I didn’t go to work last Tuesday because I was ________________________. 
 
 


 
 
Speaking Task 
 
Rick doesn’t seem to trust doctors very much. Talk about the health care system in 
your country. Is it good? Is it free for citizens or do you need to pay? How are the 
doctors in general; do they treat patients well? 
 
Record your answer at www.speakpipe.com/espressoenglish or send the MP3 to 
homework@espressoenglish.net for feedback!

1. b

8. a

4. hassle 
5. out of commission 
6. pumped 
7. on and off 
8. low-key

Lesson 39: Music Lessons 
 
Charlie goes for his violin lesson with Mr. Lee. Listen to their conversation and mark 
the statements below “True” or “False.” 
 
Listening Comprehension 
True or false according to the dialogue? 
1. Charlie didn't practice this past week because his violin was broken 
2. This week was the first time he didn't practice 
3. The music lessons with Mr. Lee are free 
4. Charlie's parents want him to learn music 
5. Charlie enjoys playing sports 
6. The winners of some music competitions earn money 
7. Charlie thinks he could win a music competition 
8. Charlie likes heavy metal rock music 
9. Mr. Lee liked country music when he was a boy 
10. Charlie approves of Mr. Lee's proposal 
11. Mr. Lee cancels today's lesson and says he will see Charlie next week 
 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Mr. Lee: Hi Charlie, nice to see you! Have you been 
practicing? 
 
Charlie: Sorry, Mr. Lee. This week has been really 
packed. 
 
Mr. Lee: That’s what you said last week. 
 
Charlie: I know it sounds like a cop-out, but it’s 
true! I had a huge science project due on Friday, plus 
I had to mow the lawn and help fix my mom’s 
sewing machine.  
 
Mr. Lee: And the week before last, you said your dog 
ate your sheet music. Honestly, Charlie, getting you 
to practice is like pulling teeth. How can you expect 
to make any headway if you don’t practice? At this 
rate, you’ll never move on to more challenging 
pieces. 
 
Charlie: I can’t help it. I’m not trying to slack off… 
it’s just that after taking care of everything else, I 
can’t seem to muster the enthusiasm to practice. 
 
packed = busy, full 
 
a cop-out = an excuse 
(usually a bad excuse 
for not taking care of 
your responsibilities) 
 
mow the lawn = cut 
the grass in the area 
around your house 
 
sewing machine = a 
household machine 
used to make, adjust, 
and repair clothes 
 
like pulling teeth = 
extremely difficult and 
painful 
 
make any headway = 
make any progress 
 
I can’t help it = I can’t 
behave any differently; 
I can’t do anything to 
change this situation 
 
slack off = be lazy 
 
muster = gather, bring 
up (an emotion) 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Mr. Lee: Your parents are paying a lot for these 
lessons, you know. But if you don’t hold up your 
end of the bargain, then they’re just pouring 
money down the drain.  
 
Charlie: To be honest, I wanted to sign up for 
baseball instead. But I already play soccer, and my 
mom says taking music classes are part of a well-
rounded education. 
 
Mr. Lee: Well, I second that. Look, I know you’re 
not crazy about learning to play the violin. But there 
has to be something we can do to make these lessons 
more bearable. 
 
Charlie: Can’t you just tell my mom that I stink at 
the violin, and I’d be better off playing sports after 
school? 
 
Mr. Lee: Well, I’m not ready to throw in the towel 
quite yet! Hmm… what about prepping for a music 
competition? Some of these competitions have cash 
prizes; that would certainly be an incentive to 
practice.  
 
Charlie: Yeah, but I wouldn’t stand a chance of 
winning. The kids who enter those competitions are 
hold up your end of

you agreed / are 
supposed to do 
 
pouring money down 
the drain = wasting 
money 
 
well-rounded = 
balanced and including 
many different areas 
 
I second that = I fully 
agree with and support 
that 
 
bearable = can be 
tolerated 
 
I stink at = I’m terrible 
at; I have no ability 
 
throw in the towel = 
give up 
 
prepping = preparing 
 
wouldn’t stand a 
chance = wouldn’t 
have a chance; it 
wouldn’t be possible 
Vocabulary 


 
 
probably super driven, like, the type to practice 5 
hours a day. And I don’t wanna be a professional 
musician or anything, I just wanna have fun. 
 
Mr. Lee: I see your point. Hey, here’s an idea – what 
kind of music do you like to listen to? 
 
Charlie: Uh, mostly rock. Not like heavy metal, 
though. I like music that has a melody. Sometimes I 
sing along. 
 
Mr. Lee: Perfect! Why don’t you give me a list of 
your favorite songs, and I’ll teach you how to play 
them? 
 
Charlie: You can play rock music on the violin?! 
 
Mr. Lee: Of course you can! Come to think of it, I 
used to do this a lot when I was your age – except it 
was with country music instead of rock. The point is, 
practicing shouldn’t feel like torture. You might as well play something you enjoy.  
 
Charlie: Yeah – that would actually be kinda cool! 
 
Mr. Lee: For today, let’s just do some exercises to get you back in the groove. At the 
end of the lesson you can write down some songs for me, and we can start working 
on them next week.

understand

or singer

and suffering on 
purpose

easily

Lesson 40: Regret 
 
Tyler, who has recently graduated from high school, is talking to his uncle Brad. Listen 
to their conversation while you try to answer the comprehension questions below: 
 
Listening Comprehension 
1. What did Brad give Tyler as a graduation gift? 
a. books 
b. a car 
c. money 
2. Where is Tyler in the college process? 
a. he hasn't applied yet 
b. he hasn't decided where he wants to go 
c. he's definitely going to the University of California 
3. Brad thinks Tyler should... 
a. listen to his parents 
b. study law 
c. take his time to decide 
4. When Brad was young, he... 
a. didn't get good grades 
b. rebelled against his parents 
c. was in a band 
5. Brad's one regret is... 
a. living a crazy lifestyle 
b. not thinking for himself 
c. losing contact with high school friends 
6. Brad also suggests that Tyler... 
a. take up a musical instrument 
b. get a girlfriend 
c. play a sport 
 


 
 
Conversation Text 
 
Brad: Hey, Tyler! How’s my favorite nephew? 
 
Tyler: Doing great, Uncle Brad! And thanks for 
the graduation gift. That cash will really come in 
handy. 
 
Brad: You’re quite welcome! So, have you 
decided what college you’re going to yet?  
 
Tyler: Um, I’m still sort of on the fence. I mean, I 
had to scramble to get all my applications in on 
time, and there wasn’t really any time to think 
about which school I really wanted to go to. I’m 
leaning toward the University of California, but 
I’m not completely sold on it… 
 
Brad: Hey, don’t get so worked up about it. You 
know, there’s no harm in taking some time off 
to mull it over.  
 
Tyler: But the clock is ticking and my mom’s 
been bugging me about the decision… 
 
Brad: Well, there’s no law that says you have to 
start college at seventeen. You could skip a year 
come in handy = be useful

and disorganized way

this decision 
 
not completely sold on it 
= not totally convinced / 
certain 
 
get so worked up = get so 
upset / agitated 
 
there’s no harm in = 
there’s nothing bad/wrong 
about 
 
mull it over = think about 
it slowly and carefully 
 
the clock is ticking = time 
is running out 
 
bugging me = annoying 
me 
 
skip = not do something 
you had originally planned 
to 
Vocabulary 


 
 
and take some time to figure out what you want in 
life. Heck, there’s no law that says you have to go to 
college at all! 
 
Tyler: With all due respect Uncle Brad, that sounds a 
little kooky. If I told my parents I wasn’t going to 
college, they’d hit the ceiling.  
 
Brad: Your parents don’t get to dictate how you live 
your life, though. I had the same problem when I was 
your age – my parents expected me to be a straight-A 
student, on the honor roll and all that. I caved to the 
pressure and I didn’t go for what I actually wanted.  
 
Tyler: Oh… that’s too bad. So what did you want? 
 
Brad: Well, it’s all in the past now. But have you ever 
heard of a band called Demon Seed? 
 
Tyler: Yeah, uh, big rock band in the 80s, right? 
 
Brad: That’s right. And guess who was supposed to 
be their drummer? 
 
Tyler: You?

hit the ceiling = get 
very angry suddenly

command/control

the best grades

the top group of 
students 
 
caved to the pressure 
= stopped resisting 
the pressure and 
decided to go along 
with it 
 
Vocabulary 


 
 
Brad: Yup, you guessed it. Those guys were my 
buddies in high school. But because I went to college, 
I had to leave the band before they made it big.  
 
Tyler: That’s cool, though! You kind of got to be a 
rock star for a while! Do you ever look back and wish 
you’d done things differently? 
 
Brad: That’s the thing, Tyler. I have no way of 
knowing how things would have turned out. It’s 
possible that I wouldn’t have been cut out for the 
rock and roll lifestyle. But I do wish I’d given it more 
thought instead of just feeling compelled to do what 
my parents wanted. 
 
Tyler: Hmm. That’s kind of sad. 
 
Brad: Well, like I said, it’s all in the past. The important thing is that you should 
learn from my mistakes. Don’t rush into anything. Make sure you’re doing it for the 
right reasons. You got that? 
 
Tyler: I sure do. Any other advice? 
 
Brad: Yeah. Learn how to play drums. It’s a lot of fun, girls love it, and you might 
even make a little money, too. 
 
Tyler: Sounds good to me! 
buddies = friends 
 
made it big = became 
very 
famous/successful 
 
look back = reflect, 
think about the past 
 
turned out = finished 
 
not cut out for = not 
compatible in 
personality and 
preferences 
 
compelled = forced, 
required, pressured
